A.io: Discuss screening tools for obstructive sleep apnea
A.q: A woman answers yes to loud snoring and to being observed to stop breathing during sleep; her body mass index is 38 kg/m2 and her shirt collar is 16 inches. She is not tired during the day, is not treated for high blood pressure and is not older than 50. What is her STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) total?
opts: Three misses one item, usually the neck: a 16-inch collar scores for anyone on this questionnaire, women included, even though the sex-specific risk factor outside it differs. Tell: count snoring, observed apnea, body mass index and neck.

Correct. Snoring 1 + observed apnea 1 + body mass index above 35 1 + neck 16 inches or larger 1 = 4; tiredness, pressure, age and gender (female) score 0. A total of 4 is intermediate, but yes to 2 of the first four questions plus a body mass index above 35 makes her high risk.

Five adds an item she answers no to: she is female, not older than 50, not tired and not treated for high blood pressure. Tell: her four positives are snoring, observed apnea, a body mass index above 35 and a 16-inch neck.

Six would need two more yes answers than she gives. Gender scores for male only, and age for older than 50 only. Tell: her positives stop at snoring, observed apnea, body mass index above 35 and a 16-inch neck, for 4.
A.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary vascular disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
A.q: A 62-year-old man with pulmonary arterial hypertension, functional class II, asks how to protect his health between visits. His resting oxygen saturation is 96%, and it falls to 87% when he walks briskly. Which recommendation should be avoided?
opts: Oxygen is recommended, especially during sleep or exertion, because hypoxia is a potent pulmonary vasoconstrictor; the goal is an arterial oxygen tension above 60 mmHg. Tell: his saturation falls to 87% on exertion, so oxygen with activity helps.
Supervised aerobic rehabilitation is safe in pulmonary hypertension and improves fatigue. Tell: it is recommended for him, not avoided; bed rest is the error.

Annual influenza and pneumococcal immunizations are mandatory in pulmonary hypertension, to prevent acute respiratory decompensations. Tell: vaccination is protective and recommended, not something to avoid.
Strict bed rest to save energy

Correct. Strict bed rest should be avoided in pulmonary hypertension: supervised, steady aerobic rehabilitation is safe, prevents muscle deconditioning and improves fatigue. Resting to spare the heart only adds deconditioning to his disease.

A.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
A.q: A 72-year-old woman has chronic respiratory acidosis from long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 68 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 35 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). A student predicts her kidneys will bring her pH back to 7.40 with time. Which statement about her compensation is accurate?
opts: It moves pH toward normal without fully correcting it

Correct. Compensation will not fully correct the pH disturbance; the underlying condition must be corrected to restore balance. Her kidneys have raised the bicarbonate to 35, which pulls the pH up toward normal, but it remains 7.33.
It overshoots, leaving her slightly alkalemic

Compensation does not overshoot into the opposite state; an alkalemic pH in a retainer would point to an added disorder. Her pH is 7.33. Tell: a simple disorder keeps the pH on the side of its primary problem.
It works through the lungs blowing off carbon dioxide

Lungs blowing off carbon dioxide compensate a metabolic acidosis. Her primary problem is respiratory, so the kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate. Tell: the compensating system is the other one.
It fully restores pH once 48 hours have passed

The chronic renal response is in place after 24 to 48 hours, but it still falls short of a normal pH; her pH is 7.33 despite years of disease. Tell: compensation narrows the gap to normal but does not close it.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 23, 34

A.topic: Aspiration, chest tube, pleurodesis and surgery
A.io: Identify medical care strategies for pleural disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 2. adult 3. elderly
A.q: A 78-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a second secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, now drained by a chest tube. His team judges that he cannot tolerate general anesthesia, so surgery is not an option. Which procedure best lowers his risk of another recurrence?
opts: Underlying pulmonary disease and recurrent pneumothorax are both contraindications to catheter aspiration. Tell: he has both, and aspiration would not prevent recurrence anyway.
ruled out by a stated finding
Thoracoscopic surgery is indicated for secondary pneumothorax and recurrence, but its risks include those of general anesthesia. Tell: his team has ruled out anesthesia, so surgery is off the table.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Most secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are treated with a chest tube and may go on to thoracoscopic surgery or thoracotomy with bleb stapling and pleural abrasion. If surgery is not an option, chemical pleurodesis via the chest tube is used: a sclerosant such as talc makes the pleural layers adhere.

Mechanical pleurodesis is manual abrasion of the pleura performed through a surgical intervention. Tell: it needs the operation he cannot have; the chemical route goes through the tube he already has.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: A 34-year-old man inhaled chlorine gas in an industrial accident. Six hours later he has severe dyspnea and bilateral infiltrates. Echocardiography is normal, and his pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 8 mmHg. Which mechanism best explains his pulmonary edema?
opts: Regurgitant flow across a heart valve
Valve lesions, such as chronic aortic or mitral regurgitation, cause cardiogenic edema with high filling pressure. Tell: his echocardiogram is normal and his wedge pressure low.
ruled out by a stated finding
Diastolic stiffening is a cardiogenic cause seen with aging and preserved ejection fraction. Tell: he is 34 with a normal echocardiogram, and his edema followed a toxic inhalation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Hydrostatic backup from the left heart
Hydrostatic backup from a failing left heart is cardiogenic edema, with a wedge pressure above 18-20 mmHg. Tell: his wedge pressure is 8 mmHg and his heart is normal on echocardiography.
ruled out by a stated finding
Toxic injury to the capillary membrane

Correct. Inhaled toxins cause chemical injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane, so the barrier shatters and protein-rich fluid leaks into the alveoli: noncardiogenic, permeability edema. His normal echocardiogram and wedge pressure of 8 mmHg exclude a pressure problem.

Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
A.q: A 46-year-old man with severe pancreatitis develops profound dyspnea on hospital day 2. His chest film shows new bilateral opacities not explained by effusion, atelectasis or nodules, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. His arterial oxygen pressure is 62 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.40. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The oxygenation criterion is a ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 62 / 0.40 = 155, well under 300, so he meets the criterion and the question becomes which class.
Mild covers ratios of 200-300 mm Hg. Tell: his ratio, 62 / 0.40 = 155, is below 200, one class worse than mild; reading 62 against 300 without dividing by 0.40 is what makes mild look right.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 62 / 0.40 = 155 mm Hg. That is under the 300 threshold and falls between 100 and 200, the moderate class. Severe pancreatitis is a systemic trigger, and his new opacities and normal heart complete the criteria.

Severe is a ratio under 100 mm Hg, the class with the most impaired oxygenation. Tell: 62 / 0.40 = 155 sits above 100, so he has not reached the severe class; an arterial oxygen pressure of 62 alone is not the ratio.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
A.q: A 63-year-old man on peritoneal dialysis develops a right pleural effusion. He has no heart failure, and his serum albumin is normal at 4.0 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.0 g/dL). He asks how the dialysis fluid in his abdomen could reach his chest. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Reduced intravascular oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia drives the effusions of nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis. Tell: his albumin is normal at 4.0 g/dL, so oncotic pressure is not the problem.
ruled out by a stated finding
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure is how heart failure causes effusion. Tell: he has no heart failure; his fluid comes from the peritoneal cavity itself.
ruled out by a stated finding

Decreased or blocked lymphatic drainage is the mechanism in malignancy and trauma. Tell: dialysis fluid reaches the chest by crossing the diaphragm through microperforations, not by blocking lymphatics.

Correct. In cirrhosis and peritoneal dialysis, increased peritoneal fluid leaks, or extravasates, across the diaphragm through microperforations into the pleural space. Peritoneal dialysis is listed among the conditions associated with transudates.

A.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
A.q: A 23-year-old man asks why trivial details of his day seem to fade after a night's sleep while what mattered stays. Which function of sleep explains this?
opts: Sleep clears metabolic waste products generated by neural activity in the awake brain; that removes chemical by-products, not information. Tell: forgetting trivia on purpose is targeted erasure of synapses, not waste clearance.
That function helps him keep information, the opposite of losing it. Tell: the fading of unimportant details is the work of targeted erasure of synapses, which keeps the synaptic network uncluttered.

Correct. One function of sleep is targeted erasure of synapses to forget unimportant information that might otherwise clutter the synaptic network. Losing trivial details while keeping what matters fits that function, which works alongside sleep's facilitation of learning or memory.

Neural maturation is a function of sleep that concerns the maturing of the nervous system, not the pruning of a day's trivia. Tell: forgetting unimportant information that might clutter the network is targeted erasure of synapses.
A.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
A.q: A 25-year-old woman has sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea at rest. Her upright chest radiograph is reviewed for a pneumothorax. Which radiographic finding establishes the diagnosis?
opts: A straight line with no meniscus marks a hemopneumothorax, where air sits above fluid in the pleural space. Tell: she has no reason for blood in the chest, and the diagnostic sign of pleural air alone is the visceral pleural line.

Blunting of the costophrenic angle is the upright-film sign of pleural fluid, 75 mL posteriorly and 175 mL laterally. Tell: a pneumothorax is air, shown by the visceral pleural line, not by a fluid-filled angle.

Bronchovascular markings are not typically visible beyond the visceral pleural edge, because only air lies there. Tell: markings past the line argue against a pneumothorax; their absence beyond a thin line supports it.

Correct. The diagnosis is established by demonstrating a visceral pleural line, the interface of lung and pleural air. It is a thin, sharp line convex outward toward the chest wall, with no bronchovascular markings visible beyond it.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
A.q: A 68-year-old man who is fit for surgery has an image-guided biopsy of a 22-mm spiculated (spiky) upper-lobe nodule that shows no malignancy. The nodule has enlarged on serial scans, and his team is concerned the biopsy missed the tumor. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Screening is for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule. Tell: he already has an enlarging, spiky nodule with a possibly false-negative biopsy, so the next move is repeat biopsy or excision.

Chemotherapy without a confirmed cancer or a stage skips the diagnosis entirely, and for non-small cell cancer it is an adjunct or stage 4 therapy. Tell: no malignancy has been proven yet, so tissue must come first, by repeat biopsy or excision.

Correct. When an image-guided biopsy does not confirm malignancy, the pathway is to consider a repeat biopsy or to proceed to excision if there is concern about a false-negative biopsy. His spiky border, upper-lobe location and growth over time are all concerning features, so a negative result does not end the workup.

Discharge treats one negative biopsy as proof, but a biopsy can miss the tumor. Tell: his nodule is spiky, in the upper lobe and enlarging, all concerning features, and a feared false negative leads to repeat biopsy or excision.

A.topic: Non-small cell treatment and targeted therapy
A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. A.q: A 67-year-old man with lung adenocarcinoma has metastases in the liver, an adrenal gland and several bones, placing him at stage 4B. Which treatment is standard for his cancer?
opts: Lobectomy belongs to earlier stages, where surgical resection is the standard for stage 1 and 2 disease. Tell: with metastases in the liver, adrenal gland and bones, removing the primary lobe cannot treat his disease.

Correct. For non-small cell lung cancer, stage 4 is treated with chemotherapy, with surgical resection considered only for a solitary metastatic lesion with a resectable primary tumor. Chemotherapy and radiation are used as adjuncts to surgery or when the patient is stage 4. He has metastases at several sites, so resection is not the plan.
Observation leaves treatable disease untreated: stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer still has a standard therapy. Tell: standard management for stage 4 is chemotherapy, not watchful waiting.

Pneumonectomy, removal of the entire lung, is a resection chosen by size and lymph involvement in operable disease. Tell: in stage 4, resection is considered only for a single metastatic lesion with a resectable primary, and he has several.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
A.q: Which nodule appearance is concerning for malignancy?
opts: Well-defined borders are a feature of benign nodules, the opposite of a spiculated edge. Tell: a crisp, smooth edge reassures, while spikes, deviations and lobulations in the border raise concern.
Popcorn calcification marks a hamartoma and sits among the benign calcification patterns with diffuse, central and concentric. Tell: popcorn calcium is benign; a spiculated border is concerning.

Fatty tissue inside a nodule points to a hamartoma, a benign lesion, as does a smoothly marginated nodule with internal fat and calcification on computed tomography. Tell: fat reassures; a spiky border worries.

Correct. A spiculated appearance, with spikes, deviations or lobulations in the border, is one of the concerning nodule features; the invasive adenocarcinoma example is a suspicious solid spiculated nodule. Other concerning features include size over 6 mm, upper lobe or hilar location and growth over time.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for pleural disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 2. adult 3. elderly
A.q: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops a spontaneous pneumothorax. His daughter, who had a pneumothorax at age 24 with no lung disease, asks how his episode is likely to differ from hers. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Good pulmonary reserve, with severe respiratory distress uncommon, describes primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a young adult without lung disease, as his daughter had. Tell: his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease removes that reserve and makes the event more dangerous.

Observation followed by discharge fits a small primary pneumothorax that stays stable on repeat film. Tell: a secondary pneumothorax is more life-threatening because of lost pulmonary reserve and calls for hospitalization for monitoring.

The physical examination is the same as in a primary episode, but the symptoms are generally greater and care is more urgent. Tell: a secondary pneumothorax, even a small one, is managed with hospitalization, unlike a stable small primary one.

Correct. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the most common cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax. The symptoms are those of a primary episode but generally greater, because the underlying disease leaves less pulmonary reserve; the event can be life-threatening and needs more immediate intervention.

A.topic: Metabolic acidosis: Winter formula and the change in anion gap
A.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 57-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome and a urinary infection has a serum albumin 2.5 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.36 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 37 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 20 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, what is her change in anion gap once the gap is corrected for albumin?
opts: This is the change in the uncorrected gap, 14 - 10. With albumin 2 g/dL below 4.5 the gap is first raised by 5 to 19, giving 19 - 10 = 9. Tell: correct for albumin before the change calculation.
Correct. Gap = 138 - (104 + 20) = 14. Albumin is 2 below 4.5, so add 2.5 x 2 = 5: corrected gap = 19. Change in gap = 19 - 10 = 9. Against a change in bicarbonate of 25 - 20 = 5, the gap rose more.
This is the uncorrected gap, 138 - (104 + 20), not a change. Correct it to 19, then subtract 10: 9. Tell: two steps, correct then subtract.
This is the corrected gap itself, 14 + 5, without subtracting the normal of 10. Change in gap = 19 - 10 = 9. Tell: the change is the distance above 10.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 50, 8, 57

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for inflammatory lung disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 11. adult 12. elderly
A.q: A 55-year-old woman is leaving the hospital after acute respiratory distress syndrome from pneumonia. She asks how long her lung function will take to recover. Which answer is accurate?
opts: One month is too soon: pulmonary function improves over 6 to 12 months after this syndrome. Tell: recovery is measured in most of a year, not weeks, and some functional deficits often remain even then.
Three months falls short of the usual course, which runs 6 to 12 months. Tell: she should expect lung function to keep improving well beyond 3 months, while some deficits may persist.

Correct. Lung function generally recovers over 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome, though functional deficits often remain, with residual diffusion deficits persisting. Physical sequelae after intensive care, such as muscle wasting, weakness and fatigue, also need attention.

Three years overshoots the typical recovery window of 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: lasting deficits can remain, but the main recovery of lung function happens within about a year.

A.topic: Identifying the disorder step by step
A.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 49-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue. Her arterial blood gas shows pH 7.40 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 40 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). A serum panel drawn at the same moment shows a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Recheck both, as the bicarbonates disagree

Correct. The bicarbonate on the blood gas and on the electrolytes is compared to verify accuracy before any further step. A difference of 10 mEq/L between samples drawn together means one result is unreliable, so neither can carry the analysis yet.
Use the panel bicarbonate and proceed
A bicarbonate of 14 with a pH of 7.40 and a carbon dioxide of 40 does not fit, and taking it on trust skips the accuracy check. Tell: verify first when the two values disagree.
Average the two values and proceed
An average of an accurate and an inaccurate value is still inaccurate. The comparison exists to catch a bad result. Tell: disagreeing values are rechecked, not blended.
Use the gas bicarbonate and proceed
Choosing one value skips the accuracy check, and the analysis could rest on the wrong number. Tell: two simultaneous bicarbonates that disagree are a warning to verify, not a choice to make.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 56, 57

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
A.q: Popcorn calcification in a lung nodule points to which lesion?
opts: Correct. Benign nodules tend to have well-defined borders and may contain fatty tissue or calcifications; popcorn-looking calcification means a hamartoma, a connective tissue growth. On computed tomography a hamartoma is a smoothly marginated solid nodule with internal fat and calcification.

Adenocarcinoma appears as a suspicious solid spiculated nodule in the periphery, and the calcification patterns grouped as malignant are ground-glass and eccentric. Tell: popcorn calcification sits on the benign side of the chart.

A carcinoid tumor is one of the rare lung tumor types, and a bronchial carcinoid is the lung source of carcinoid syndrome; popcorn calcification is not its described sign. Tell: popcorn calcification is the hamartoma pattern.

A healed granuloma, an inflammatory lesion, is the smoothly marginated nodule with central calcification, not popcorn calcification. Tell: a central dot of calcium suggests a granuloma; popcorn clusters suggest a hamartoma.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: A 28-year-old man has had mild left-sided chest wall pain for a day, reproduced by pressing on a rib cartilage. His Wells score is 0, and the clinician's gestalt for pulmonary embolism is very low (under 15%). His heart rate is 78/min and oxygen saturation 99%. He has no hemoptysis, takes no estrogen, has never had a clot, has had no recent surgery or trauma and has no leg swelling. Applying the PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria), which step fits?
opts: A ventilation-perfusion scan is imaging for patients who need imaging but cannot have contrast. Tell: he needs no imaging at all, because the rule-out criteria are fully met.
Computed tomographic angiography follows a positive D-dimer or a Wells score above 4. Tell: he has neither; he passes every rule-out criterion.

Correct. He meets all eight criteria: age under 50, heart rate under 100, saturation above 94%, no hemoptysis, no estrogen, no prior venous thromboembolism, no surgery or trauma and no unilateral leg swelling. With very low gestalt and every criterion met, the workup stops.
Order a D-dimer to be safe

The D-dimer is for low- or intermediate-probability patients who fail the rule-out criteria, and its low specificity invites false positives. Tell: he passes all eight criteria, so no D-dimer is needed.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
A.q: A 44-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has respiratory events on polysomnogram that occur when he sleeps on his back and not when he lies on his side. He wants a measure to add to his care. Which therapy targets this pattern?
opts: Nasal steroids treat nasal congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: he has no nasal symptoms; his events depend on his body position.

Correct. Positional therapy fits when events occur in the supine position: a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps him lying on his side. His events are confined to back-sleeping, the exact pattern it addresses.

Palatal implants are for mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: nothing says he cannot tolerate pressure therapy, and his events are tied to position.

Tracheostomy is a cure because it bypasses the site of upper airway obstruction, but it is a surgical airway. Tell: his events depend on body position, which a sleep belt or shirt addresses without surgery.
A.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 12, 13

A.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
A.q: A 35-year-old man's 8-hour sleep recording is scored stage by stage. Which stage takes up the largest share of his total sleep time?
opts: Correct. Stage N2 makes up the majority of the sleep cycle and is the longest stage by total duration. Rapid eye movement sleep fills about 25% of a young adult's sleep, and stage N2 outlasts both the brief drowsy stage N1 and the deep stage N3, so it holds the largest share of his night.

Rapid eye movement sleep occupies about 25% of a young adult's sleep time, roughly a quarter of the night. Tell: the stage that makes up the majority of the sleep cycle and the longest by total duration is stage N2, not the dream state.

Stage N1 is the brief, drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep. Tell: a transition stage does not make up the bulk of the night; stage N2 is the majority of the sleep cycle and the longest stage by total duration.

Stage N3 is the deepest, most restful non-rapid eye movement stage, and it decreases with age. Tell: depth is not duration; the stage that is the longest by total duration and fills the majority of the cycle is stage N2.
A.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 13, 28, 9

A.topic: Normal values and the anion gap
A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 41-year-old woman has bipolar disorder treated with lithium and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Routine testing shows sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 106 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), albumin 4.4 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL), and no monoclonal protein. Which part of her history best accounts for her anion gap?
opts: A plasma cell dyscrasia lowers the gap through a cationic monoclonal protein. Her testing shows no monoclonal protein. Tell: the stem removes this cause and leaves her lithium.
ruled out by a stated finding
A low albumin is the usual reason for a low gap, but her albumin is 4.4 g/dL, normal, so there is nothing to correct for. Tell: check the albumin first; when it is normal, look for an added cation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Metformin is a cause of raised-gap metabolic acidosis, which would push the gap above 12 and lower the bicarbonate. Her gap is 4 and her bicarbonate 26. Tell: metformin raises the gap; hers is low.

Correct. Her gap is 136 - (26 + 106) = 4, below the normal 6 to 12. A decreased gap comes from added abnormal cations such as lithium, which are not counted in the formula. Her normal albumin and absent monoclonal protein remove the other low-gap causes.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 48

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
A.q: A 65-year-old woman with a biopsy-proven 4-cm non-small cell carcinoma has a staging scan showing metastases in the right adrenal gland and in several vertebrae. Which stage is her cancer?
opts: Stage 3B rests on lymph node spread, such as supraclavicular or scalene nodes with a smaller tumor, without metastasis. Tell: adrenal and bone lesions are distant metastases, which place her in stage 4.

Stage 3C is a tumor larger than 5 cm with spread to supraclavicular or scalene nodes or the far side's nodes, but no metastasis. Tell: her adrenal and bone lesions are distant spread, and every stage 1 to 3 cancer is M0.

Stage 4A allows spread within the chest to the other lung, pleura, pericardium or surrounding fluid, or to just one site outside the chest, such as one adrenal gland. Tell: she has two sites outside the chest, adrenal and bone, which is stage 4B.

Correct. Multiple extrathoracic metastases, in one or more organs, are scored M1c, and spread to multiple sites outside the chest, such as the adrenal gland and bones, is stage 4B. Any tumor size and any node status still give stage 4B once the cancer has reached several sites beyond the chest.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: Which World Health Organization pulmonary hypertension group includes connective tissue disease, human immunodeficiency virus infection and schistosomiasis?
opts: Correct. Group 1, pulmonary arterial hypertension, is pre-capillary disease with an obliterative and proliferative mechanism. Its causes are idiopathic disease, connective tissue disease, human immunodeficiency virus infection and schistosomiasis.

Group 2 is post-capillary pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease, a passive obstruction to pulmonary venous outflow, as in heart failure or mitral stenosis. Tell: group 2 is the left heart; infections and connective tissue disease sit in group 1.

Group 3 is pulmonary hypertension from lung disease or hypoxia: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease and sleep apnea. Tell: group 3 needs a lung or breathing disorder, and the listed conditions are arterial causes.

Group 5 holds unclear or multifactorial causes with a complex mechanism, such as hematologic, systemic and metabolic disorders like sarcoidosis. Tell: group 5 is the catch-all; idiopathic and connective tissue causes define group 1.

A.topic: Pulmonary embolism: risk factors and presentation
A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: A 55-year-old woman with a confirmed large pulmonary embolism has an electrocardiogram showing a deep S wave in lead I and a Q wave with an inverted T wave in lead III (S1Q3T3). What does this pattern indicate?
opts: S1Q3T3 has low sensitivity, so most patients with embolism do not show it, and its absence rules nothing out. Tell: it is highly specific, a sign of severe right ventricular strain, not a screen.
Left ventricular hypertrophy does not produce a deep S in lead I with Q and T changes in lead III. Tell: a large embolism loads the right ventricle, and S1Q3T3 is its strain pattern.

An inferior infarction gives Q waves across the inferior leads with ST change, not a deep S wave in lead I. Tell: the S1Q3T3 pattern in a patient with a large embolism points to right ventricular strain.

Correct. S1Q3T3 suggests severe right ventricular strain rather than embolism as such: it is highly specific but has low sensitivity. In a patient with a large embolism, it reflects the acutely loaded right ventricle.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for inflammatory lung disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 11. adult 12. elderly
A.q: Which measure belongs to the supportive care of an adult with coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
opts: Hemoglobin targets are a critical care question in acute respiratory distress syndrome, where transfusion at 7 g/dL is used because higher targets do not improve outcomes. Tell: chronic coal dust care is oxygen, vaccines, rehabilitation and cessation.
Lavage to remove the coal dust

No effective curative treatment is available, and lavage is a diagnostic study rather than a way to clear the dust. Tell: nothing clears or cures the disease, so care is oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation.

Routine pulmonary artery catheters belong to acute respiratory distress syndrome care, where they are avoided because they offer no clinical benefit. Tell: a catheter is an intensive care device, not part of chronic dust-disease support.

Correct. Supportive care for coal workers' pneumoconiosis includes oxygen, pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, because no effective curative treatment is available. Lung transplant may be indicated in severe cases.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
A.q: A 71-year-old man with a 60 pack-year history has 2 months of cough, wheezing and blood-streaked sputum. Computed tomography shows a central mass arising in the right main bronchus, and sputum cytology shows malignant cells. Which lung cancer type is most likely?
opts: Small cell carcinoma is also central, but it infiltrates the mucosa and is usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis. Tell: catching the tumor on sputum cytology is the feature of squamous cell carcinoma, the central bronchial tumor diagnosable from sputum.

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma sits centrally and often originates in a bronchus, has the strongest association with smoking, and causes cough, wheezing and hemoptysis once it obstructs the bronchus. Unlike the other lung cancers it can be caught with sputum testing, so malignant cells in his sputum from a central bronchial mass point to it.

Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery as a large cavitated mass and spreads to unusual sites such as the bowel. Tell: a central bronchial mass caught on sputum cytology points to squamous cell carcinoma instead.
Adenocarcinoma usually forms in the mid-lung and periphery, often near peripheral scars. Tell: his mass is central in a main bronchus and shed malignant cells into his sputum.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 61-year-old woman takes hydrocortisone for a chronic inflammatory condition and must stay on a corticosteroid. She has a metabolic alkalosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.49 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which change to her corticosteroid is most appropriate?
opts: Keep hydrocortisone at the same dose
Hydrocortisone has more mineralocorticoid activity, which drives the alkalosis, so leaving it unchanged keeps the contributor in place. Tell: change the steroid or lower the dose.
A higher dose adds mineralocorticoid effect and worsens the alkalosis; the advice is to decrease the dose if possible. Tell: dose goes down, not up.

Correct. If a patient with metabolic alkalosis requires corticosteroids, lower the dose or change to one with less mineralocorticoid activity: prednisone or methylprednisolone rather than cortisone or hydrocortisone.
Cortisone sits with hydrocortisone on the side to move away from, with more mineralocorticoid activity. Tell: the preferred agents are prednisone and methylprednisolone.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 53, 54, 55

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
A.q: A 61-year-old woman with a body mass index of 43 kg/m2, hypersomnolence and a raised serum bicarbonate is being evaluated for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Which test is the gold standard for her?
opts: Sleep study with oxygen saturation alone

Oxygen saturations feed the screening features, such as an overnight lowest saturation under 80%, but they do not measure carbon dioxide. Tell: the gold standard adds continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring to polysomnography.

An awake arterial blood gas shows the carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg that the criteria require, but it is a daytime measurement. Tell: the named gold standard is the overnight study with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.

A home kit assesses obstructive sleep apnea and is set aside when there is awake hypoventilation. Tell: the gold standard for this syndrome is polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.
Sleep study with carbon dioxide monitoring

Correct. Polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring is the gold standard for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Following carbon dioxide through the night captures the hypoventilation of the syndrome alongside the obstructive events that coexist in about 90% of patients.
A.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 32, 31, 30, 8

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
A.q: A 66-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed lung cancer is meeting a radiation oncologist. Her son has read that some lung cancers respond far better to radiotherapy than others, and he asks which type benefits most. Which response is accurate?
opts: Correct. Small cell carcinoma responds better to chemotherapy and radiation than the three non-small cell cancers, and radiation works best when it is in limited stage. Non-small cell cancers do not respond well to chemotherapy or radiation, which serve as adjuncts to surgery or for stage 4.

Squamous cell carcinoma is a non-small cell cancer, and these do not respond well to chemotherapy or radiation, which serve as adjuncts to surgery or for stage 4. Tell: the type singled out for a better response is small cell carcinoma.

Large cell carcinoma has no standardized treatment because of its variety and rarity, and as a non-small cell type it responds poorly to radiation. Tell: radiotherapy benefits small cell carcinoma most, especially in limited stage.

Adenocarcinoma is a non-small cell cancer, and these respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiation, which are adjuncts to surgical resection. Tell: the cancer that responds better to radiation is small cell carcinoma.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary nodules and neoplasms in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
A.q: An 83-year-old woman who still smokes has a 60 pack-year history. She has no symptoms and no known lung nodule. Her daughter asks whether she should start yearly lung cancer screening scans. Which describes her eligibility?
opts: Correct. Screening is recommended for adults 55 to 80 with at least a 30 pack-year history who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years. Her 60 pack-years and current smoking would qualify, but at 83 she is beyond the upper age limit of 80.
There is no 5-year screening interval: eligible people are screened annually with low-dose chest computed tomography. Tell: she is not eligible at all, because the age range stops at 80.
Smoking now does not disqualify anyone: the criteria include current smokers and those who quit within the last 15 years. Tell: her age, 83, is what places her outside the range.
Current smoking and 60 pack-years meet two criteria, but the age range ends at 80. Tell: at 83 she falls outside the screening window despite her heavy smoking.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
A.q: A first primary spontaneous pneumothorax has an apex-to-cupola distance greater than 3 cm with significant dyspnea and chest pain. Which treatment is listed?
opts: Observation with oxygen fits a small pneumothorax, under 3 cm, with no or minimal symptoms. Tell: large size plus significant symptoms takes observation off the table.

Correct. A moderate or large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, more than 3 cm at the apex, with moderate or severe symptoms such as significant chest pain and dyspnea, is treated with chest tube insertion. A recurrent primary pneumothorax instead goes to thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis.
Open thoracotomy is kept for complicated cases, and thoracoscopic surgery has largely supplanted it. Tell: an uncomplicated first large pneumothorax is drained with a chest tube, not opened.

Thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis is the treatment when a primary pneumothorax recurs, and this is a first episode. Tell: first and large means chest tube; recurrent means surgery with pleurodesis.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
A.q: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 2 days of sharp, well-localized pain over the left chest wall that worsens with deep breathing, coughing and sneezing. She is tachypneic, with limited chest wall expansion on the left. A pleural friction rub (a grating, creaking sound) is heard in both phases of respiration and disappears when she holds her breath. Her chest radiograph is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Costochondritis, inflammation of the costal cartilage, is among the other causes of chest pain to consider after the dangerous ones. Tell: her friction rub comes from inflamed pleural layers rubbing together with each breath, a pleural sign that cartilage inflammation does not explain.

Pericarditis is one of the dangerous causes to consider first, and breath holding is the test that separates a pericardial friction rub from a pleural one. Tell: her rub disappeared when she held her breath, which marks it as pleural, not pericardial.

Correct. Pleurisy is inflammation of the parietal pleura, and inflammatory disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus are among its causes. Well-localized sharp pain made worse by breathing, coughing and sneezing, limited expansion on the affected side and a pleural friction rub fit, and a rub that disappears with breath holding comes from the pleura.

A pneumothorax also brings acute pleuritic pain, but its examination is hyperresonance with diminished breath sounds, and its film shows a visceral pleural line. Tell: her chest radiograph is normal and she has a friction rub, not the quiet, hyperresonant chest of pleural air.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology: a. Sarcoidosis b. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) c. Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders (CTD) 3. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
A.q: Which imaging finding is characteristic of silicosis?
opts: Pleural plaques with linear streaking at the bases are the most common radiographic finding of asbestosis, not silicosis. Tell: plaques on the pleura point to asbestos, while calcified rims of the hilar nodes point to silica.

Diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on computed tomography is the idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis picture. Tell: honeycombing beneath the pleura means idiopathic fibrosis; nodules with eggshell hilar calcification mean silica.

A normal heart size with air bronchograms in bilateral infiltrates is the imaging of acute respiratory distress syndrome, an acute illness rather than a dust disease. Tell: acute confluent infiltrates mean distress syndrome; eggshell nodes mean silica.

Correct. Silicosis imaging shows nodular opacities throughout, silicotic nodules of 1 to 10 mm forming nodular pulmonary fibrosis, and eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes.

A.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
A.q: A 28-year-old woman lies relaxed with her eyes closed at lights-out and then sleeps on into her deepest non-rapid eye movement stage. Which sequence of dominant waves is her electroencephalogram expected to show?
opts: This runs the night backward: delta waves mark the deepest stage, which she reaches last, and alpha marks the relaxed wakefulness she starts in. Tell: the tracing slows progressively into sleep, from alpha to delta.

Beta belongs to alert wakefulness with the eyes open, yet she starts relaxed with her eyes closed, and this sequence stops before the deepest stage. Tell: the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage ends in delta waves.

Correct. Relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed shows alpha waves; stages N1 and N2 show theta waves; and stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, shows delta waves. The frequency of the tracing becomes progressively slower as she passes from rest into deep sleep.

Beta waves come with alert, active processing and with rapid eye movement sleep, not on the way down from relaxation into deep sleep. Tell: frequency slows progressively into non-rapid eye movement sleep, so the middle step is theta.
A.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 28, 27, 29

A.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
A.q: After many hours of activity, activating-system neurons fatigue and their feedback loop with the cortex fades. What happens next?
opts: Rapid eye movement sleep starts at once

A night opens with non-rapid eye movement stages that descend toward deep sleep, and rapid eye movement episodes come later, recurring about every 90 minutes. Tell: the transition is into sleep generally; rapid eye movement sleep arrives later in each cycle.

Release of the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition starts wakefulness when the sleep centers are not activated. A fatigued activating system with fading feedback heads the opposite way, into sleep. Tell: fatigue leads to sleep; release leads to waking.

Correct. With the activating neurons fatigued and the positive feedback between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fading, the sleep-promoting centers take over and the brain makes the transition from wakefulness to sleep.

The transition described is from wakefulness to sleep, and sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by stimuli. Coma is unconsciousness without arousal and is not the normal end of a long day. Tell: fatigue of the activating system brings sleep, not coma.
A.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 7, 9, 19

A.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
A.q: A 33-year-old woman's partner notices that late in the night her eyes dart rapidly under closed lids, her breathing becomes irregular and her fingers twitch. When woken, she describes a vivid dream. Which stage was she in?
opts: Stage N3 is deep, restful non-rapid eye movement sleep, with slow heart rate, decreased breathing and less vivid dreams. Tell: darting eyes, irregular breathing and a vivid dream mark rapid eye movement sleep, not the deepest non-rapid stage.

Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep is the active form of sleep associated with vivid dreaming, rapid eye movements, irregular muscle movements, and irregular heart rate and breathing. Late-night timing fits too, since rapid eye movement periods lengthen in the later cycles.

Quiet wakefulness is a relaxed, awake state with alpha waves, but she had to be woken and was dreaming. Tell: she was asleep, and a vivid dream with rapid eye movements and irregular breathing is the dream state of rapid eye movement sleep.
ruled out by a stated finding

Stage N2 is deeper non-rapid eye movement sleep with heart rate and temperature falling, and non-rapid eye movement dreams are less vivid and often not remembered. Tell: irregular breathing and darting eyes are rapid eye movement features.
A.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 13, 14, 7, 28

A.io: Discuss relationship between small cell lung cancer and paraneoplastic syndromes.
A.q: A 64-year-old man with a 50 pack-year history has a central lung mass, and biopsy shows small cell carcinoma. Over 2 months he has developed progressive muscle weakness, worst in his legs. Testing confirms Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (autoimmune muscle weakness, particularly in the legs). He asks what causes the weakness. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: The antibodies target the nerve side of the neuromuscular junction, not the muscle fibers themselves. Tell: calcium channels on the nerve endings stop working, too little acetylcholine is released, and the muscles cannot contract properly.
Low sodium from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone causes confusion, seizures and ataxia. Tell: his diagnosis is an antibody attack on calcium channels at nerve endings, not an electrolyte effect.

Correct. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a rare autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks calcium channels on nerve endings at the neuromuscular junction. The non-functioning channels prevent release of acetylcholine, so the muscles cannot contract properly, producing progressive weakness, particularly in the legs.

Spinal cord compression comes from bone metastasis to the spine. Tell: his weakness has an autoimmune cause at the neuromuscular junction, where antibodies disable calcium channels on nerve endings and too little acetylcholine is released.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: A 64-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic hypoxemia has a hematocrit of 58% (normal 41-50%). Echocardiography shows right ventricular hypertrophy. How does his blood count add to the load on his right ventricle?
opts: Correct. Chronic hypoxia drives polycythemia, and the extra red cells raise blood viscosity and the workload of the heart. That compounds the structural and hypoxic rise in pulmonary resistance his right ventricle already pumps against.

More red cells make blood thicker, not thinner; viscosity rises with the hematocrit. Tell: his hematocrit is above the normal range, the polycythemia of chronic hypoxia, which raises resistance to flow.

Extra red cells do not dilate the pulmonary arteries; in chronic lung disease the vessels are constricted by hypoxia and lost to structural damage. Tell: polycythemia adds to his load by thickening the blood, on top of the narrowed vascular bed.
Polycythemia is the body's answer to low oxygen and raises the oxygen the blood can carry. Tell: its cost is thicker blood and more cardiac work, which is how it compounds his right ventricular load.

A.topic: Connective tissue and other unknown-cause disease
A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology: a. Sarcoidosis b. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) c. Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders (CTD) 3. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
A.q: A 57-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken methotrexate for 6 years. She now has progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. She asks whether her arthritis medicine could be involved. Which response is accurate?
opts: Yes, methotrexate can cause this disease

Correct. Methotrexate is used for many autoimmune diseases, including lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, and it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Rheumatoid arthritis is itself a connective tissue cause, so her disease and her treatment both belong in the differential.

Methotrexate, a common treatment for rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, is in the treatment-related group of interstitial lung disease causes. Tell: her years of methotrexate are a recognized cause of exactly this disease, so the medicine cannot be dismissed.
Yes, methotrexate deposits dust in the lungs

Dust deposition in the alveoli is how silica and coal cause pneumoconiosis, through macrophage invasion and fibrosis. Tell: methotrexate is a drug cause in the treatment-related group, not an inhaled dust, so the mechanism offered is wrong.
No, drug injury needs cancer chemotherapy

The drug causes reach beyond chemotherapy: the treatment-related group includes methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin as well as chemotherapeutics. Tell: methotrexate is named in that group in its own right, whatever disease it is given for.

A.topic: Metabolic acidosis: causes and the anion gap
A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 55-year-old woman has received large volumes of normal saline for 3 days after abdominal surgery. She also takes acetaminophen for pain, has nasogastric suction, and takes a loop diuretic for edema. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 115 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of her care should be limited?
opts: Gastric suction removes acid and causes a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis. Her pH is 7.32 with a low bicarbonate. Tell: suction pushes the pH up, so it is not feeding this acidosis.

Correct. Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 140 - (15 + 115) = 10, normal, with a high chloride. Saline infusion is a normal-gap cause, so the infusion feeding the acidosis is the part to limit.
Acetaminophen toxicity causes a raised-gap acidosis through 5-oxoproline. Her gap is 10, normal. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride fits saline, not acetaminophen.
Diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. Her bicarbonate is 15. Tell: a diuretic raises the bicarbonate; hers has fallen.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 45, 46, 53

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: A 61-year-old man has abdominal bloating, early satiety, profound fatigue and an episode of syncope while climbing stairs. His lungs are clear on auscultation. His chest film shows enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning, and right heart catheterization shows an elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure with a wedge pressure of 10 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: An acute embolism strikes suddenly, over minutes to hours, with dyspnea, pleuritic pain or collapse. Tell: his bloating, early satiety and enlarged central arteries with pruning describe a chronic right-sided process.
Left heart failure brings orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, bibasilar crackles, Kerley B lines and a high wedge pressure. Tell: his lungs are clear and his wedge pressure is 10 mmHg.
ruled out by a stated finding

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema floods the alveoli, with crackles, pink frothy sputum and a high wedge pressure. Tell: his lungs are clear and his wedge pressure is normal, so fluid is not backing up from the left heart.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Bloating, early satiety, profound fatigue and exertional syncope with clear lungs are right heart failure. Enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning, and a normal wedge pressure with a high mean pulmonary artery pressure, confirm a pre-capillary, right-sided process.

A.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 58-year-old woman in the intensive care unit with septic shock is febrile, hypotensive and breathing 32 times a minute. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.40 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 20 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorders are present?
opts: Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis

Correct. Gap = 138 - (104 + 12) = 22, raised, so a metabolic acidosis is present despite the normal pH. Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, range 24 to 28; her 20 is below it, so a concurrent respiratory alkalosis is present. Sepsis is the classic setting, and the two pull the pH back to normal.

A respiratory disorder alone never produces a large anion gap; her gap of 138 - (104 + 12) = 22 places a primary metabolic acidosis in the picture. Tell: when the gap is high, a metabolic acidosis is present whatever the carbon dioxide does.
Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation

Appropriate compensation would leave carbon dioxide within 24 to 28 (1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, plus or minus 2). Hers is 20, lower than compensation alone explains, and compensation never brings the pH fully back to 7.40. Tell: a normal pH with a raised gap means a second process.
Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis

A concurrent respiratory acidosis would put carbon dioxide above the predicted 24 to 28. Hers is 20, below the range, which is the opposite pattern. Tell: above the Winter range means respiratory acidosis, below it means respiratory alkalosis.
A.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 26, 28, 49

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: A 50-year-old woman has progressive exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography estimates a high pulmonary artery systolic pressure with an enlarged right ventricle, and her chest film, pulmonary function tests and ventilation-perfusion scan are normal. Which test is required to confirm pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension?
opts: Correct. Right heart catheterization is the mandatory confirmation: it measures the mean pulmonary artery pressure, the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance. A high mean pressure with a normal wedge pressure confirms pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension.

B-type natriuretic peptide reflects ventricular stretch and helps separate cardiogenic dyspnea from pulmonary mimics. Tell: it cannot measure the pulmonary pressures or the wedge pressure that confirm pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension.

Computed tomographic angiography images the pulmonary arteries for clot but measures no pressures. Tell: her normal perfusion scan has already excluded the clot group, and the pressures still need direct measurement.

Echocardiography is the screening test, the most useful initial study, and it estimates pressures rather than measuring them. Tell: confirmation needs direct measurement of the mean pressure and wedge pressure, which catheterization provides.

A.topic: Interstitial lung disease: presentation and workup
A.io: Identify medical care strategies for inflammatory lung disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 11. adult 12. elderly
A.q: A 76-year-old man has had interstitial lung disease for 9 years, and his dyspnea now occurs at rest. An echocardiogram shows right heart failure. What does the right heart failure indicate about his lung disease?
opts: It is at an early stage

Early disease may show a normal examination and exertional symptoms only. Tell: dyspnea at rest and right heart failure are features of progression and advanced disease, the opposite end of his 9-year course from the early stage.
It has entered an acute phase

An acute presentation develops over days to weeks, while most interstitial lung diseases present chronically over months to years. Tell: a 9-year course ending in right heart failure is chronic, advanced disease, not a new acute phase.
It is at an advanced stage

Correct. Right heart failure appears with advanced interstitial lung disease, and dyspnea that has spread from exertion to rest also marks progression. Early in the disease the examination may be normal, so these findings place him late in a long, chronic course.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema displays cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement and batwing perihilar opacities, a hydrostatic problem of the heart rather than scarred lung. Tell: his right heart failure follows 9 years of lung disease, the pattern of advanced interstitial disease.

A.topic: Pulmonary embolism: risk stratification and treatment
A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
A.q: Which pulmonary embolism risk category is normotensive but shows right ventricular dysfunction or elevated troponin?
opts: Transient or provoked risk (recent surgery, trauma, hospitalization, estrogen therapy) belongs to the 3-month anticoagulation decision, not the acute severity category. Tell: provoked versus unprovoked sets duration; low, submassive and massive set severity.

Correct. Submassive, or intermediate-risk, embolism is normotensive (systolic blood pressure above 90) but shows right ventricular dysfunction on echocardiography or computed tomographic pulmonary angiography, or myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin or B-type natriuretic peptide). It carries a high risk of sudden deterioration.

Massive, high-risk embolism requires sustained hypotension (systolic below 90 for more than 15 minutes), pulselessness or profound bradycardia. Tell: this patient is normotensive, so the category cannot be massive.
ruled out by a stated finding

Low-risk embolism is normotensive with no right ventricular dysfunction and negative cardiac biomarkers, giving an excellent prognosis with standard anticoagulation. Tell: right ventricular dysfunction or a positive biomarker lifts a normotensive patient out of low risk.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology: a. Sarcoidosis b. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) c. Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders (CTD) 3. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
A.q: A 55-year-old farmer with farmer's lung has stopped handling moldy hay, but he remains hypoxic with cyanosis, tachypnea and tachycardia, and his disease is judged severe. Which treatment may be helpful now?
opts: Return to work with a mask

Continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state, so going back to the hay keeps the cause in play. Tell: the first step is to identify and avoid the agent, and severe disease then adds corticosteroids.

Correct. After the agent is identified and avoided, corticosteroids may be helpful in severe cases of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, with other immunosuppressants and supportive care such as oxygen. His persistent hypoxia, cyanosis, tachypnea and tachycardia despite avoidance mark severe disease.

Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on mechanical ventilation. Tell: his disease is a hypersensitivity reaction to hay, where severe cases call for corticosteroids.

High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit even in acute respiratory distress syndrome, where it is listed to avoid. Tell: his severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis calls for corticosteroids, not a ventilator mode.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
A.q: A 43-year-old woman with habitual snoring and daytime sleepiness has a home sleep apnea test that does not show obstructive sleep apnea. Her symptoms persist. What is the best next step?
opts: Correct. At-home kits will not always diagnose mild obstructive sleep apnea; they are most helpful in moderate to severe disease. A negative home study in a woman with ongoing snoring and sleepiness therefore needs a polysomnogram, which can also find other sleep disorders a home kit cannot assess.

Stimulants such as modafinil treat sleepiness but carry headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and treating the symptom would skip the study that could find mild disease.

Repeating the same kind of study repeats its limits: home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea alone and can miss mild disease. Tell: the polysomnogram is the study that measures severity across sleep stages and positions.
A negative home study does not exclude mild disease, since home kits will not always diagnose it. Tell: her symptoms persist, so the question stays open until a polysomnogram answers it.
