D.topic: Pulmonary embolism: risk stratification and treatment
D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 71-year-old man with a massive pulmonary embolism has had a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg for 25 minutes. He also has active bleeding from a duodenal ulcer, with black stools and a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL). Which intervention fits?
opts: Correct. Massive embolism with sustained hypotension needs immediate advanced intervention, but active bleeding is an absolute contraindication to thrombolytics. Mechanical thrombectomy or surgical embolectomy physically removes the clot without a drug that would worsen his bleeding.

Anticoagulation alone is too slow for massive embolism with 25 minutes of hypotension. Tell: massive embolism needs immediate advanced intervention, and for him that means removing the clot physically.

Transfusion replaces lost blood but does not remove the contraindication: his ulcer is still actively bleeding. Tell: thrombolysis would turn an active bleed into a catastrophic one, so the clot must be removed physically.
ruled out by a stated finding

Catheter-directed thrombolysis delivers the same clot-dissolving drug class closer to the clot, and it still carries major bleeding risk. Tell: active bleeding contraindicates thrombolytics by any route.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
D.q: Which treatment for sleep-disordered breathing is itself a risk factor for central sleep apnea?
opts: Correct. Patients using continuous positive airway pressure are among those at risk for central sleep apnea. The same therapy is still the first device to consider in central sleep apnea, with adaptive servo-ventilation if it fails.
Positional therapy with a sleep belt

Positional therapy treats obstructive events that occur when supine, with a belt or shirt that keeps a lateral position; it is not a risk factor for central apnea. Tell: the pressure therapy, not the positional one, carries that risk.

An oral appliance is an obstructive apnea option that fails in severe disease or without teeth; it is not named as a risk factor for central apnea. Tell: the device on the central apnea risk list delivers continuous positive airway pressure.

A nasal expiratory resistance device uses the patient's own breathing to make expiratory positive airway pressure; it is not named as a central apnea risk factor. Tell: the risk sits with continuous positive airway pressure.
D.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 12, 24, 26

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
D.q: A 57-year-old man has 5 days of fever, cough with purulent sputum and right pleuritic chest pain, and a right pleural effusion is tapped. Pleural fluid protein is 4.4 g/dL with serum protein 7.2 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 240 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 210 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). Which is the most likely cause of the effusion?
opts: Correct. Protein ratio 4.4 / 7.2 = 0.61, above 0.5; lactate dehydrogenase ratio 240 / 210 = 1.14, above 0.6; fluid lactate dehydrogenase 240 exceeds two-thirds of 280, about 187. The fluid is an exudate, pneumonia is the most common cause of exudative effusion, and fever with purulent sputum and pleuritic pain is its clue set.
Nephrotic syndrome causes a transudate by lowering oncotic pressure as albumin is lost. Tell: his protein ratio of 0.61 and lactate dehydrogenase values mark an exudate, which fits his pneumonia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Cirrhosis with ascites causes a transudate, through peritoneal fluid crossing the diaphragm and low oncotic pressure. Tell: his fluid is exudative by every criterion, and he has fever with purulent sputum.
ruled out by a stated finding

Heart failure causes more than 90% of transudates, with edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Tell: his fluid meets all three of Light's criteria, an exudate, and his story is an infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
D.q: A 29-year-old man settles into bed in a sleep laboratory, and a few minutes later he is drowsy and drifting off into light sleep. Which stage is he in?
opts: Stage N3 is the deepest, most restful non-rapid eye movement stage, with delta waves and tissue growth and repair. Tell: he is only drowsy and drifting off, which is the light transition stage, stage N1, not the deepest one.

Stage N2 is less responsive, deeper sleep, with heart rate and temperature falling, and it is the longest stage by total duration. Tell: drowsiness at the edge of wakefulness, minutes after lying down, is stage N1.

The first rapid eye movement period comes at the end of the first 90- to 120-minute cycle, after the non-rapid eye movement stages. Tell: a few minutes after lying down he is still in the drowsy transition, stage N1.

Correct. Stage N1 is the transition from wakefulness: the person is somnolent or drowsy and in light sleep. Minutes after settling into bed and drifting off, he fits this first non-rapid eye movement stage, before the deeper stages N2 and N3.
D.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 28, 27, 6, 7

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
D.q: A 47-year-old man had a traumatic hemothorax that was only partly drained, and a collection of blood remains in his pleural space weeks later. Which complication does this retained blood most directly risk?
opts: Chylothorax follows thoracic duct disruption, most often from trauma such as thoracic surgery, and fills the space with chyle. Tell: retained blood does not become chyle; it becomes a nidus for infection.

Correct. Undrained blood collections serve as a primary nidus for infection, and a retained hemothorax leads directly to empyema, as well as fibrothorax and trapped lung. That is why tube thoracostomy, the essential first step, aims to evacuate the blood.
Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinal tissues after alveolar rupture or esophageal perforation. Tell: blood left in the pleural space risks infection, not mediastinal air.
Tension pneumothorax is trapped air under a one-way valve with hypotension and tracheal deviation. Tell: retained blood is fluid, and its risk is infection of that fluid.

D.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
D.q: A 31-year-old woman has been breathing rapidly for 30 minutes during a panic attack. She has not vomited, has no diarrhea and takes no medicines. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.54 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her potassium is 3.3 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Which process best accounts for her potassium level?
opts: Severe depletion of total body potassium

Severe potassium depletion is a saline-unresponsive cause of metabolic alkalosis, with a high bicarbonate. Her bicarbonate is 23 and her low carbon dioxide drives the pH, and nothing in her history removes potassium from the body. Tell: her potassium has moved, not been lost.
Potassium lost through the gut from vomiting

Vomiting causes a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. She has not vomited, and her bicarbonate is 23 with a low carbon dioxide, a respiratory picture. Tell: the stem rules out vomiting.
ruled out by a stated finding
Potassium shifted out of cells as hydrogen ions entered
That is the shift of acidosis, and it raises the serum potassium. Her pH is 7.54, alkalemic, so potassium moves the other way. Tell: a low potassium with a high pH is the alkalosis shift into cells.
Potassium shifted into cells as hydrogen ions left them

Correct. A pH of 7.54 with a carbon dioxide of 28 is a respiratory alkalosis from anxiety. In alkalosis hydrogen ions shift out of cells and potassium shifts into cells, resulting in hypokalemia, with no potassium actually lost from the body.

D.topic: Pulmonary embolism: risk factors and presentation
D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: What is the Palla sign on a chest film in pulmonary embolism?
opts: A central, perihilar distribution of alveolar edema is the batwing pattern of pulmonary edema, not a sign of embolism. Tell: batwing means flooded alveoli; Palla means an enlarged pulmonary artery.
Focal peripheral oligemia, decreased vascularity, is the Westermark sign. Tell: Westermark is a loss of vessels; Palla is an enlarged vessel.

Correct. The Palla sign is an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery. With the Westermark sign and Hampton's hump it is a classic chest film clue, highly suggestive of pulmonary embolism but infrequent; most films in embolism are abnormal but nonspecific.
A wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity indicating infarction is Hampton's hump. Tell: Hampton is the wedge at the pleura; Palla is the enlarged artery.

D.topic: Interstitial lung disease: presentation and workup
D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology: a. Sarcoidosis b. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) c. Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders (CTD) 3. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
D.q: Which chest radiograph finding points to sarcoidosis or silicosis among the interstitial lung diseases?
opts: Correct. On chest radiography, hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy points to sarcoidosis or silicosis. Sarcoidosis shows symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy, and silicosis can calcify the periphery of the hilar nodes in an eggshell pattern.

A normal heart size with air bronchograms and bilateral infiltrates that become confluent is the imaging of acute respiratory distress syndrome, not of a chronic granulomatous or dust disease. Tell: acute confluent infiltrates mean distress syndrome; enlarged nodes mean sarcoidosis or silicosis.

Pleural plaques are the most common chest radiograph finding in asbestosis, seen with linear streaking at the bases. They do not point to sarcoidosis or silicosis. Tell: pleural plaques mean asbestos; enlarged hilar nodes mean sarcoidosis or silicosis.

Diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing is the computed tomography picture of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, a late fibrotic finding. Tell: honeycombing means established fibrosis, while enlarged hilar and mediastinal nodes point to sarcoidosis or silicosis.

D.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
D.q: A 32-year-old woman's recording during a period of rapid eye movements shows irregular, high-frequency waves, and the technician labels it desynchronized sleep. What does that label describe?
opts: Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep is also called desynchronized sleep because there is a lack of synchrony in neuron firing when there is brain activity. The tracing is irregular and high frequency, much like an awake, active person's, which fits her period of rapid eye movements.

Fatigue of neurons in the activating system is the proposed trigger for falling asleep after many hours awake, not a description of a tracing. Tell: desynchronized describes how neurons fire during rapid eye movement sleep, without synchrony.

Rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 per second in a relaxed, awake person are alpha waves of quiet wakefulness. Tell: her waves are irregular and high frequency during sleep with rapid eye movements, which is the desynchronized pattern, not a rhythm.

This is the reverse of the label: desynchronized means a lack of synchrony in neuron firing. Tell: her irregular, high-frequency tracing reflects neurons firing out of step with each other, not together.
D.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 29, 22, 19

D.topic: Metabolic acidosis: causes and the anion gap
D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 45-year-old man has renal tubular acidosis, irritable bowel syndrome with intermittent diarrhea, and glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. His roommate found him confused beside an open container of antifreeze. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.23 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 22 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 9 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 105 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 9 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Diarrhea causes a normal-gap acidosis by gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, with a high chloride. His gap is 26. Tell: bicarbonate loss leaves the gap normal; a toxin adds unmeasured anions.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause a normal-gap acidosis by loss of bicarbonate. His gap of 26 needs a raised-gap cause. Tell: this drug is on the normal-gap list, not the toxin list.

Correct. Low pH with a bicarbonate of 9 is a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 140 - (9 + 105) = 26, well above 12. Ethylene glycol is a toxic alcohol on the raised-gap list. His other conditions all cause a normal-gap acidosis.

Renal tubular acidosis causes a normal-gap acidosis through chloride retention, with a gap of 6 to 12 and a high chloride. His gap is 26 and his chloride 105. Tell: calculate the gap before choosing a list.
D.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 44, 45, 46, 47

D.io: Discuss screening tools for obstructive sleep apnea
D.q: A 58-year-old man with loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness is seen for evaluation before elective surgery. He has never been tested for sleep apnea. Which property makes the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire suited to this visit?
opts: It confirms the diagnosis before surgery

A questionnaire estimates risk; obstructive sleep apnea is confirmed on a polysomnogram, with 5 or more obstructive events per hour plus symptoms, or 15 or more. Tell: the score places him in a risk group and does not replace the sleep study.

Severity is measured during a sleep study: a split-night polysomnogram records the first 2 hours of sleep to determine severity. Tell: the questionnaire gives a low, intermediate or high risk of having the disease, not a grade of disease he has.

Correct. The questionnaire has been used as a preoperative evaluation tool for people without a known diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea who may be at risk for perioperative complications, and it has the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires. A highly symptomatic patient in a high-risk setting is where it has value.

The questionnaire is singled out for the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires, the property that suits catching at-risk patients before surgery. Tell: its strength is not missing people at risk, which is sensitivity, not specificity.
D.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 16, 17, 8, 9

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 57-year-old man has severe obstructive sleep apnea and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, with nocturnal hypoxemia. Echocardiography shows a normal left ventricle and an enlarged right ventricle, and his ventilation-perfusion scan is normal. Which World Health Organization pulmonary hypertension group fits?
opts: Group 1, pulmonary arterial hypertension, is the diagnosis reached after lung disease and clot are excluded. Tell: he has two Group 3 causes, so his pressure is explained by lung disease and hypoxia.
Group 2 is pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease, with a high wedge pressure and abnormal left-sided findings. Tell: his left ventricle is normal on echocardiography.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Lung disease and hypoxia make up Group 3, and both of his conditions are on that list: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and sleep apnea, with its chronic nocturnal alveolar hypoventilation. Alveolar hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vessels and loads his right ventricle.
Group 4 is chronic thromboembolic disease, shown by segmental defects on a ventilation-perfusion scan. Tell: his scan is normal, which excludes the clot group.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic respiratory acidosis from kyphoscoliosis is intubated, and the ventilator lowers her carbon dioxide from 70 to 40 mm Hg within an hour. Her bicarbonate is 35 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which complication is she now at risk for?
opts: Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys have raised bicarbonate over days, and it falls slowly. Lowering carbon dioxide rapidly leaves that bicarbonate unopposed, and the alkalosis may cause cardiac arrhythmias, reduced cerebral perfusion and seizures.
Alkalosis increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and decreases delivery to tissues. Her sudden alkalosis worsens delivery. Tell: alkalosis holds oxygen on hemoglobin.

Her retained bicarbonate of 35 is unopposed once the carbon dioxide falls, which produces alkalosis, not acidosis; a high bicarbonate after high carbon dioxide is the post-hypercapnia pattern. Tell: the leftover bicarbonate makes her alkalotic.

Potassium leaves cells in acidosis. A rapid fall in her carbon dioxide with a bicarbonate of 35 creates an alkalosis, which moves potassium into cells and lowers it. Tell: the risk after over-correction is alkalosis, so think low potassium.
D.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 34, 37, 5

D.topic: Normal values and the anion gap
D.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 54-year-old man with chronic kidney failure has fatigue. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.29 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
opts: This uses a normal bicarbonate of 24 in place of his measured 14: 138 - (24 + 103) = 11. The formula takes the measured value, which is 14. Tell: plug in the patient's own bicarbonate, not the normal one.

Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (bicarbonate + chloride) = 138 - (14 + 103) = 138 - 117 = 21, above the normal 6 to 12. A raised gap with a low pH and low bicarbonate is a raised-gap metabolic acidosis, and renal failure is on that list.

This adds his potassium of 4.0 to the sodium: (138 + 4) - (14 + 103) = 25. The anion gap formula used here is sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate, with no potassium. Tell: potassium is not part of the calculation.
This subtracts only the chloride: 138 - 103 = 35, leaving out the bicarbonate. The gap subtracts both measured anions, chloride and bicarbonate. Tell: two anions come off the sodium, not one.
D.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 26, 45

D.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
D.q: A 37-year-old woman believes that sleep matters for the brain and nothing else. Which statement about the physiological effects of sleep is accurate?
opts: The effects of sleep are physiological, on the nervous system and on other body systems, including blood pressure, heart rate, breathing and metabolic rate. Tell: a measurable 10 to 30% fall in these values during non-rapid eye movement sleep is not psychological.

Muscle tone does change in sleep, being very depressed in rapid eye movement sleep, but the two major types of effects are on the nervous system and on the other functional systems. Tell: the brain is one of the two targets, not left out.

That leaves out half of the picture: sleep also has effects on other functional systems of the body, such as the fall in blood pressure, heart rate and metabolic rate in non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: there are two types of effects, nervous system and body.
It affects brain and body systems

Correct. Sleep has two major types of physiological effects: effects on the nervous system and effects on the other functional systems of the body. Its functions span both, from neural maturation and cognition to conservation of metabolic energy, so its importance is not limited to the brain.
D.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 17, 12, 10

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
D.q: A 63-year-old woman who still smokes and has a 50 pack-year history has had 6 weeks of hemoptysis and has lost 4 kg. She saw an advertisement and asks to enroll in a lung cancer screening program. Which plan should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Screening is for high-risk individuals without symptoms or a known nodule. Hemoptysis and weight loss are symptoms that should be worked up for possible lung cancer now, with computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen followed by biopsy, so screening would delay her diagnosis.

A comprehensive metabolic panel including calcium is part of the laboratory workup, beside a complete blood count with differential and alkaline phosphatase. Tell: these laboratory studies support her diagnostic workup and are appropriate.

Computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen is the standard study for symptoms of possible lung cancer. Tell: she needs exactly this diagnostic scan, so it is not the plan to avoid.

Biopsy follows the contrast scan in the standard workup, by bronchoscopy, a transthoracic approach or thoracoscopy depending on location. Tell: tissue diagnosis is a needed step for a symptomatic patient, not one to avoid.

D.topic: Metabolic acidosis: Winter formula and the change in anion gap
D.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A metabolic acidosis shows pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 25 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What does the carbon dioxide indicate?
opts: Inadequate compensation means the carbon dioxide has not fallen far enough, sitting above the Winter range. Here it has fallen too far. Tell: an overshoot below the range is a respiratory alkalosis.

Appropriate compensation would place the carbon dioxide at 33 to 37 for a bicarbonate of 18. A value of 25 overshoots, and compensation never pushes the pH past normal to 7.48. Tell: below the Winter range is a second disorder.
A concurrent respiratory acidosis would leave the carbon dioxide above 33 to 37. Here it is 25, below. Tell: higher than predicted adds acidosis; lower than predicted adds alkalosis.

Correct. Winter formula: 1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35, range 33 to 37. The measured 25 is below the range, so the lungs are removing more carbon dioxide than compensation requires: a concurrent respiratory alkalosis, which also explains the alkaline pH.
D.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slide 49

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
D.q: A 27-year-old man has a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax. On his upright chest radiograph, the apex-to-cupola distance is 4 cm and the interpleural distance at the level of the hilum is 1.5 cm. How is its size classified by the American College of Chest Physicians definition?
opts: The hilum distance is the British landmark, not the one the American definition reads. Tell: the American College of Chest Physicians label of large comes from the 4 cm apex-to-cupola distance.
The apex-to-cupola distance is the right landmark, but small means under 3 cm. Tell: his apex-to-cupola distance is 4 cm, past the 3 cm cutoff, so the pneumothorax is large.
The interpleural distance at the level of the hilum is the British guideline measurement, not the American one. Tell: the American definition reads the apex-to-cupola distance, which is 4 cm here.

Correct. The American College of Chest Physicians sizes a pneumothorax by the apex-to-cupola distance: under 3 cm is small, 3 cm or more is large. His 4 cm apex-to-cupola distance makes it large; the interpleural distance at the hilum is the British guideline measurement.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
D.q: A 41-year-old woman has daytime sleepiness, and her partner reports habitual snoring and pauses in her breathing. Her polysomnogram shows 8 predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour, and her symptoms are not explained by another condition, a medication or a substance. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Not diagnostic until 15 events per hour
15 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour confirm the diagnosis without any symptom. Tell: she has symptoms, so the lower threshold of 5 events per hour applies, and her 8 events meet it.

Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed with 5 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour plus a symptom such as sleepiness, or habitual snoring and breathing interruptions noted by a bed partner, when no other condition, medication or substance explains them. She has 8 events and those symptoms.

Central sleep apnea shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion, airflow stopping because effort stops. Tell: her events are predominantly obstructive, the defining feature of obstructive sleep apnea.
Indeterminate until a home kit is done

A home kit will not always diagnose mild disease and adds nothing after a polysomnogram has answered the question. Tell: her result already meets the criterion of 5 or more events per hour with symptoms.
D.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 8, 26

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 41-year-old woman has idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and is not vasoreactive on testing. She is in functional class II with stable symptoms and no signs of right ventricular failure. Which treatment approach fits her?
opts: Correct. Patients who are not vasoreactive are stratified by risk, and low or intermediate risk (class II or III) calls for oral combination therapy: an endothelin receptor antagonist with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. Starting the combination early is superior to sequential monotherapy.
Calcium channel blockers belong to vasoreactive patients. Tell: her vasoreactivity test was negative, which sends her to risk stratification and the targeted oral classes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Parenteral prostanoids are for high-risk patients: class IV or rapid clinical decline. Tell: she is class II and stable, so oral combination therapy is the right step.
Sequential monotherapy, starting one drug and adding another later, is the approach early combination has outperformed. Tell: low- or intermediate-risk patients start with both oral classes together.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
D.q: A 27-year-old woman is being discharged after her primary spontaneous pneumothorax has resolved. She has a flight booked for a conference and asks for advice about air travel. Which advice is accurate?
opts: Air travel is delayed, not forbidden for life. Tell: the guide is to wait after resolution and confirm it with a film; avoiding scuba diving is the lasting restriction.
Fly once the chest pain is gone
Pain relief does not show that the lung has fully re-expanded. Tell: the advice is a delay after resolution, with resolution confirmed on a chest X-ray, not judged by symptoms.
Delay flying; confirm with a film

Correct. Air travel is delayed for 7-14 days after resolution, and resolution is confirmed with a chest X-ray before she flies. Follow-up films verify complete lung re-expansion, and she is also counseled on recurrence and, if she smokes, on stopping.
Fly if her oxygen level is normal
A normal oxygen saturation does not confirm that the pneumothorax has resolved. Tell: the check before flying is a chest X-ray showing re-expansion, after a waiting period.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 72-year-old man has had interstitial lung disease for 8 years, and his right ventricle has been known to be hypertrophied. Over the past month his exertional dyspnea has worsened. Which new finding shows that his right ventricle has decompensated?
opts: Pink frothy sputum signals alveolar flooding in cardiogenic pulmonary edema, from high left-sided pressure. Tell: right ventricular decompensation congests the systemic veins and organs, not the alveoli.

Flattened diaphragms mark hyperinflation from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on the chest film. Tell: he has interstitial lung disease, which restricts rather than hyperinflates, and a lung film finding says nothing about right ventricular decompensation.

Orthopnea with bibasilar crackles is left-sided failure, fluid backing into the lungs from a failing left heart. Tell: his load is on the right ventricle from lung disease, and its failure shows in the liver, abdomen and legs.

Correct. When a chronically hypertrophied right ventricle decompensates, its elevated diastolic pressure transmits backward: the liver congests and becomes tender, ascites forms and pitting edema spreads in dependent areas. A right ventricular heave, an intensified P2 and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur go with it.

D.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
D.q: Which wave does the electroencephalogram show in stage N2?
opts: Sawtooth waves are part of the mixed, low-voltage pattern of rapid eye movement sleep, not of a non-rapid eye movement stage. Tell: sawtooth waves mean rapid eye movement sleep.
Delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second and high in voltage, mark stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage. Stage N2 has not slowed that far. Tell: N3 is delta; N2 is theta.

Beta waves mark the awake, eyes-open state and rapid eye movement sleep, whose waves resemble wakefulness. Stage N2 is slower. Tell: as non-rapid eye movement sleep deepens, the frequency slows away from beta.

Correct. Stage N2, the less responsive, deeper sleep that is the longest stage by total duration, shows theta waves, 4 to 7 cycles per second, on the electroencephalogram. Delta waves wait for stage N3.
D.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 25, 28

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
D.q: A 73-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a 65 pack-year history has worsening cough, wheezing and hemoptysis. Computed tomography shows a central mass in a main bronchus with cavitation and a spiculated (spiky) border. Which noninvasive test can sometimes catch this tumor type, unlike the other lung cancers?
opts: A chest film is not a good tool for working up a suspicious nodule or symptoms. Tell: computed tomography has already shown the mass, and of the lung cancers it is squamous cell carcinoma that can be caught with sputum.

A mucicarmine stain is done on biopsy tissue and shows mucin production, which relates to adenocarcinoma. Tell: it needs tissue, so it is not noninvasive, and mucin points to a peripheral tumor rather than a central bronchial one.

Correct. A central, cavitating bronchial mass in a heavy smoker with cough, wheezing and hemoptysis is the picture of squamous cell carcinoma, which unlike the other lung cancers can be caught with sputum testing. Sputum cytology is not sensitive in general, so tissue biopsy is still the standard.

A serum calcium can show hypercalcemia, a paraneoplastic finding seen particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, but it does not identify the tumor. Tell: the noninvasive test that can catch the tumor cells themselves is sputum cytology.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
D.q: Where is the needle placed for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax?
opts: The needle goes in on the thoracic side of the pneumothorax; the opposite side is where the mediastinum has been pushed. Tell: decompress the side with the trapped air.

Correct. The typical needle decompression site is on the thoracic side of the pneumothorax, in the 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, at the midclavicular line. Patient body habitus can change the choice, which is why this is called the typical site.

The midaxillary line belongs to the chest tube site in the 4th or 5th intercostal space; the 2nd-space needle goes in at the midclavicular line. Tell: the needle sits high and in front, the tube lower and to the side.
Under the third rib, midclavicular line
The needle passes over the 3rd rib, in the 2nd intercostal space, not under it. Tell: 'over the 3rd rib' is written into the site, the same landmark used for catheter aspiration.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
D.q: A 67-year-old man with small cell lung carcinoma diagnosed 2 months ago has a dull ache under his right ribs, poor appetite and yellowing of his eyes. Exam shows an enlarged liver with a firm edge. Which complication has developed?
opts: Adrenal metastasis causes adrenal insufficiency with fatigue, dizziness, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Tell: yellowing of the eyes and a firm, enlarged liver point to liver involvement instead.

Bone metastasis causes bone pain, fractures without falls and spinal cord compression. Tell: his complaints are a right upper quadrant ache, jaundice and a firm enlarged liver, which localize the spread to the liver.

Correct. Small cell carcinoma is metastatic, to the liver, bone or brain, before detection in over 70% of patients. Liver metastasis causes a dull right upper quadrant ache, hepatomegaly with a firm edge, lack of appetite, jaundice and eventually hepatic failure, matching his findings.

Brain metastasis presents with headaches, vision changes, vomiting, syncope or seizures and papilledema. Tell: jaundice and a firm enlarged liver are hepatic findings, and he has no neurologic complaints.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology: a. Sarcoidosis b. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) c. Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders (CTD) 3. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
D.q: A 63-year-old former shipyard worker undergoes lung biopsy, which shows ferruginous bodies (a histologic result of inorganic dust inhalation) within fibrotic interstitium. What does this finding suggest?
opts: Sarcoidosis tissue shows noncaseating granulomas, and active disease raises the erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Tell: ferruginous bodies come from inorganic dust inhalation, matching his shipyard asbestos exposure rather than granulomas.

Mesothelioma is diagnosed from pleural fluid cytology in a patient with an effusion. Tell: a ferruginous body marks significant exposure, not cancer; mesothelioma remains a risk, about 10% over a lifetime in asbestos workers.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis histology shows interstitial lymphocytes and plasma cells with non-caseating granulomas, from organic dust. Tell: ferruginous bodies come from inorganic dust, the opposite category, as in his shipyard work.

Correct. A ferruginous body is a histologic finding in interstitial lung disease that results from inorganic dust inhalation, and in tissue it suggests significant asbestos exposure. His years in shipyards are a listed asbestos setting, with insulation, demolition and construction.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary nodules and neoplasms in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
D.q: An 81-year-old woman with severe heart failure is unfit for surgery. Computed tomography shows a growing 2.5-cm nodule lying against a large blood vessel, and the interventional radiologist judges image-guided biopsy unsafe. Positron emission tomography shows intense uptake in the nodule and no lymph node or distant spread. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Waiting a year leaves a growing, intensely avid nodule untreated in a patient who still has a nonsurgical option. Tell: when biopsy is unsafe in an unfit patient, the pathway proceeds directly to stereotactic ablative or conventional radical radiotherapy, or radiofrequency ablation.
Biopsy is done in unfit patients when it is possible and safe. Tell: her radiologist judged it unsafe, and the pathway allows treatment without tissue in exactly that situation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Wedge resection with frozen section is a surgical route for fit patients. Tell: she is unfit for surgery because of severe heart failure, so resection of any size is off the table.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. For a patient unfit for surgery, image-guided biopsy is the next step only if it is possible and safe. When biopsy is not possible or not safe, the pathway goes straight to stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation or conventional radical radiotherapy, so her unsafe biopsy does not block treatment.

D.topic: Interstitial lung disease: definition and causes
D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
D.q: A 71-year-old man has taken amiodarone for atrial fibrillation for 6 years. Over several months he has developed progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough and bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern. He has no occupational exposures. How is his interstitial lung disease classified?
opts: The occupational group of known cause includes asbestosis and silicosis, which need years of work exposure to asbestos fibers or silica dust. Tell: he has no occupational exposure; the known cause in his history is a medicine he takes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Granulomatous lung disease covers sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where organized granulomas form in response to inflammation. Tell: nothing in his history points to granulomas or an inhaled organic antigen; his medicine list points to a drug cause.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the diagnosis only when no associated cause is evident, even in a patient over 65 with crackles and restriction. Tell: amiodarone is an associated cause in his history, so his disease cannot be called idiopathic.

Correct. Amiodarone sits with radiation, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics in the treatment-related group of interstitial lung disease of known cause. His exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restrictive pattern fit interstitial disease, and his years of amiodarone supply the cause.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
D.q: A 63-year-old woman has a biopsy-proven 2-cm non-small cell carcinoma in the right upper lobe. On exam a firm right supraclavicular lymph node is palpable, and its biopsy shows the same cancer. Imaging shows no metastasis to other organs. Which stage is her cancer?
opts: Stage 2B with a small tumor allows spread only to peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes on the same side. Tell: a supraclavicular node is N3, and N2 or N3 involvement automatically moves a cancer to stage 3.
Stage 3A with a small tumor means spread to the same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes. Tell: a supraclavicular node reaches farther, N3, which places a tumor of 5 cm or less in stage 3B.

Correct. Spread to any supraclavicular or scalene node is N3, which moves a cancer to stage 3. With a tumor no more than 5 cm, spread to supraclavicular or scalene nodes, or to mediastinal or hilar nodes on the side without the tumor, is stage 3B. Her 2-cm tumor with a positive supraclavicular node fits.

Stage 4A is spread to the other lung, the pleura or pericardium, the fluid around the lungs or heart, or one site outside the chest. Tell: a supraclavicular node counts as lymph node involvement, not distant metastasis, and no other organ is involved.

D.io: Discuss relationship between small cell lung cancer and paraneoplastic syndromes.
D.q: A 70-year-old woman with known small cell lung carcinoma has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L (normal 135-145) and low serum osmolality from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone. Her family asks why her legs and lungs show no swelling if her body is holding on to too much water. Which response is accurate?
opts: Her sodium is 124, well below the normal floor of 135, and her osmolality is low. Tell: water retention dilutes the sodium; the lack of edema comes from the insidious course, not from a high sodium.
ruled out by a stated finding

Her low sodium and low osmolality come from retaining too much water under excess antidiuretic hormone, the opposite of dehydration. Tell: the absence of edema reflects the slow, insidious course, not a fluid deficit.

Correct. In small cell lung cancer, neuroendocrine tumor cells produce excess antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), and the body retains too much water, lowering serum sodium and osmolality. The result is confusion, seizures, ataxia and other neurologic dysfunction, but no signs of peripheral or pulmonary edema, because the process is insidious over time.

Edema is not part of this picture: the syndrome produces neurologic dysfunction without peripheral or pulmonary edema, because it develops insidiously. Tell: watch instead for confusion, seizures and ataxia as the sodium falls.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
D.q: A 53-year-old man has loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness, and his primary care clinician suspects obstructive sleep apnea. Which referral is part of his care?
opts: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea raises cardiovascular risks such as hypertension, arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death at night, but the referral named for the sleep disorder is a sleep physician. Tell: he is being evaluated for the apnea itself.
Maxillomandibular advancement is one of many surgical options for established disease. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, and the referral named in patient education is to a sleep physician.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it is a surgical option rather than the referral named for a suspected diagnosis. Tell: the named referral is to a sleep physician, with proper counseling.

Correct. Patient education for obstructive sleep apnea includes referral to a sleep physician, together with proper counseling. His snoring, witnessed apneas and sleepiness make the diagnosis likely, and confirming it takes a sleep study.
D.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 15, 13, 18

D.topic: Metabolic acidosis: Winter formula and the change in anion gap
D.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: How is the change in anion gap calculated?
opts: Six is the bottom of the normal range of 6 to 12. Using it inflates the change in gap. Tell: the accepted normal gap is 10.

Correct. Change in anion gap = calculated anion gap minus a normal gap, with 10 the accepted value. It is then compared with the change in bicarbonate, measured from an accepted normal of 25; the two should be equal in a simple metabolic acidosis.
Twelve is the top of the normal range of 6 to 12, not the value used for the change. Tell: the accepted normal for the calculation is 10, the average of the range.
Twenty-five is the accepted normal for bicarbonate, used for the change in bicarbonate. Tell: the gap uses 10; the bicarbonate uses 25.
D.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 27, 50, 7

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
D.q: After a response to initial therapy, which lung cancer is offered prophylactic cranial irradiation?
opts: Adenocarcinoma is non-small cell and is treated by stage, with resection in early stages and chemotherapy in stage 4. Tell: preventive irradiation of the brain belongs to the small cell pathway.

Large cell carcinoma is kept apart from small cell carcinoma precisely because their treatments differ, and it has no standardized treatment. Tell: prophylactic cranial irradiation is a small cell treatment.
Squamous cell carcinoma is a central non-small cell type whose management combines surgery, chemotherapy and radiation. Tell: the brain is irradiated preventively in small cell carcinoma.

Correct. In small cell carcinoma with a complete or partial response to initial therapy, prophylactic cranial irradiation is recommended in limited stage and considered, with or without thoracic radiotherapy, in extensive stage. Brain magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred scan of the brain.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
D.q: A 26-year-old woman has a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Her respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and she speaks in whole sentences. How is she classified by the American College of Chest Physicians stability definition?
opts: The heart-rate criterion is over 60 and under 120 beats per minute. Tell: her heart rate of 96 sits inside that range, so tachycardia has not crossed the cutoff of 120, and her other values pass as well.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Every criterion is met: respiratory rate 20, under 24; heart rate 96, between 60 and 120; normal blood pressure; room-air saturation 96%, over 90%; and whole sentences. Stability requires all of these, and she has all of them.
The respiratory-rate criterion is under 24 breaths per minute. Tell: her rate of 20 meets it, and her heart rate, pressure, saturation and speech pass too, so nothing makes her unstable.
ruled out by a stated finding
The saturation criterion is a room-air oxygen saturation over 90%. Tell: her 96% on room air clears it, and her respiratory rate, heart rate, pressure and whole sentences meet the other criteria.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
D.q: A 52-year-old man has acute bird fancier's lung from the pigeons he keeps at home, and his symptoms are settling. He asks whether he can keep the birds if he takes medicine whenever symptoms flare. Which counsel is accurate?
opts: Continued exposure may worsen his disease

Correct. Prompt diagnosis is key so the patient can be removed from the irritating environment: symptoms can be reversible if caught early, but continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state. Treatment starts with identifying and avoiding the agent, here his birds.
His lung damage is already permanent

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis symptoms can be reversible if caught early, and acute disease shows little change on imaging. Tell: his acute illness is settling, so his outcome still depends on removing the birds now.

Corticosteroids may help severe cases, but treatment starts with avoiding the agent. Tell: no medicine is described as making continued exposure safe, and continued exposure may worsen the disease toward its chronic form.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a non-atopic, non-asthmatic inflammatory disease from inhaled organic dust. Tell: his reaction is to the bird antigen itself, so treating it as asthma leaves the exposure in place.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 39-year-old man has had nasogastric suction for 4 days after bowel surgery and has dry mucous membranes. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.50 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 48 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His potassium is 3.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L), and his urine chloride is low. Along with stopping the suction, which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: He is already volume depleted, and diuretics are themselves a cause of saline-responsive alkalosis. Tell: a low urine chloride with dry mucous membranes calls for fluid, not fluid removal.

Correct. Gastric suction causes a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, confirmed by the low urine chloride, and he is volume depleted. Treatment is to stop contributors such as suction and treat the fluid and potassium deficits.
Ventilation to lower his carbon dioxide
His carbon dioxide of 48 is compensation for the alkalosis. Lowering it would raise the pH further. Tell: treat the metabolic cause, not the compensation.
Corticosteroids are a contributor to metabolic alkalosis and are among the drugs to stop, and hydrocortisone has more mineralocorticoid activity than prednisone. Tell: steroids worsen this alkalosis.
D.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 53, 54

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 70-year-old man has acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. He is sitting upright on high-flow oxygen and has received an intravenous loop diuretic, but he remains tachypneic with an oxygen saturation of 87%. He is alert and able to protect his airway. Which step comes next?
opts: A fluid bolus raises preload and capillary hydrostatic pressure, the engine of cardiogenic edema. Tell: his lungs are flooded, so more fluid would worsen them.

Correct. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation is the P in the toolbox: it mechanically stents flooded alveoli open, pushes fluid back across the membrane and lowers intrathoracic preload and afterload. He is alert and can protect his airway, and oxygen with diuresis has not been enough.
Morphine is a use-with-caution agent that risks respiratory depression, and it does nothing for failing oxygenation. Tell: his hypoxemia needs positive pressure to stent his alveoli open.
Upright positioning is part of treatment, because gravity reduces venous return; lying flat increases it. Tell: lying him flat would push more blood toward his congested lungs.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 67-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic cor pulmonale. His electrocardiogram shows peaked P waves, severe right axis deviation and a tall R wave in lead V1. Which chamber change does the tall R wave in V1 indicate?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy is not a result of lung disease, and his tracing shows severe right axis deviation, a right-sided pattern. Tell: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease loads the right ventricle, and the tall R wave in V1 reflects that right-sided thickening.

Correct. A tall R wave in V1 is the electrocardiogram sign of right ventricular hypertrophy, the thickened chamber of chronic cor pulmonale. His peaked P waves point to right atrial enlargement, and severe right axis deviation goes with the chronic disease.

Left atrial enlargement comes from left-sided pressure and shows in the P wave, not the R wave. Tell: his peaked P waves and right axis deviation are right-sided, and the tall R in V1 is right ventricular hypertrophy.
Right atrial enlargement is real in him, but its electrocardiogram sign is the peaked P wave. Tell: the question asks about the tall R wave in V1, which belongs to the ventricle, not the atrium.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary vascular disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
D.q: A 56-year-old woman has 2 days of mild pleuritic chest pain. Her Wells score is 0, and the clinician's gestalt for pulmonary embolism is very low. Her heart rate is 84/min and oxygen saturation 98%. She has no hemoptysis, takes no estrogen, has no prior clots, has had no surgery or trauma and has no leg swelling. Applying the PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria), which step fits?
opts: Stopping requires all eight criteria to be true, and the first is age under 50. Tell: at 56 she cannot pass, however well she looks.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. She fails one criterion, age under 50. A patient with a Wells score of 4 or less who fails any rule-out criterion goes to a D-dimer: a negative result rules embolism out, and a positive one leads to imaging. She passes every other item.
A ventilation-perfusion scan is imaging for patients who need imaging but cannot have contrast. Tell: she needs a D-dimer first; imaging follows only if it is positive.
Computed tomographic angiography follows a positive D-dimer or a Wells score above 4. Tell: her Wells score is 0, so the D-dimer comes before any imaging.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following inflammatory lung diseases: 2. Interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology: a. Sarcoidosis b. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) c. Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders (CTD) 3. Interstitial lung disease of known etiology: a. Occupational lung diseases 4. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis 5. Pneumoconiosis 6. Asbestosis 7. Silicosis 8. Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia 9. Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
D.q: A 57-year-old stone worker has had silicosis for 8 years. He asks which complication his lung disease puts him at increased risk of. Which is it?
opts: Mesothelioma, a primarily pleural cancer, is nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, with a 10% lifetime risk in asbestos workers. Tell: his dust is silica from stone work, whose listed complications are tuberculosis, massive fibrosis and scleroderma.

Correct. Silicosis carries an increased risk of tuberculosis, together with progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. That is why patients with silicosis should have a tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film, and why the risk deserves mention at follow-up.

Goodpasture syndrome is glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in young adults, identified by basement membrane antibodies. Tell: it is not a silica complication; silicosis raises the risk of tuberculosis.

Hypercalcemia occurs in about 5% of patients with sarcoidosis and is an indication for corticosteroids there. Tell: silica dust causes silicosis, not sarcoidosis, and silicosis complications are tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma.

D.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
D.q: A 30-year-old woman wakes in the morning and stays awake through the day without effort. According to the proposed sleep-wake theory, what keeps her wakefulness going once it begins?
opts: Increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure and slow heart rate, belongs to non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: it is a feature of sleep, not the loop that sustains wakefulness, which is reticular-cortex positive feedback.

Wakefulness begins when the sleep centers are not activated, which releases the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition. Tell: active sleep centers would favor sleep, not sustain her waking day; the positive feedback loop does that.

Correct. Once wakefulness begins, it can sustain itself naturally because of a positive feedback mechanism: the reticular activating nuclei excite the cerebral cortex and peripheral nervous system, which send positive feedback signals back to the same nuclei and keep them active.

Fatigue after many hours awake is what ends wakefulness: the feedback cycle fades and the sleep-promoting centers take over. Tell: fatigue closes the waking day; positive feedback between the reticular nuclei and the cortex carries it.

Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
D.q: A 68-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 3 years ago and has heart failure with an ejection fraction of 25%. He now has ankle edema and distended neck veins, and echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle. Right heart catheterization shows an elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 27 mmHg. How is his right-sided failure classified?
opts: Correct. A wedge pressure of 27 mmHg shows high left-sided filling pressure, and his failing left ventricle (ejection fraction 25%) is pushing pressure back into the lungs. Left heart disease, including heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, is World Health Organization Group 2, the passive post-capillary group, and Group 2 is not cor pulmonale.

Group 1 is pulmonary arterial hypertension from obliterative remodeling of the small arteries (idiopathic, connective tissue disease, schistosomiasis), a pre-capillary group with a normal wedge pressure. Tell: his wedge pressure of 27 mmHg places the problem after the capillaries, in the left heart.
ruled out by a stated finding

Group 4 is chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, an obstructive pre-capillary group from unresolved clot. Tell: he has no clot history, and his high wedge pressure points to the left heart, not to blocked pulmonary arteries.

Cor pulmonale is right ventricular change caused exclusively by a primary lung or pulmonary vascular disorder, with a normal wedge pressure. Tell: his wedge pressure is high and his cause is a failing left ventricle, which is exactly what must be excluded before calling it cor pulmonale.

D.q: A 52-year-old man with acute respiratory distress syndrome from diffuse pneumonia is on low tidal volume ventilation. His arterial oxygen pressure is 80 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.50, and an echocardiogram has excluded cardiogenic edema. Which intervention decreases mortality at his severity?
opts: Transfusion is given at a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, and higher hemoglobin targets do not improve patient outcomes. Tell: raising hemoglobin is not the mortality-lowering step at a ratio of 160; prone positioning is.

Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit, and echocardiography has already assessed his heart. Tell: monitoring with a catheter does not lower mortality; early prone positioning does at his moderate severity.

Correct. His ratio is 80 / 0.50 = 160 mm Hg, moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome. Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe cases, so he qualifies, alongside the low tidal volume ventilation he is already receiving.

High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit and is listed among approaches to avoid. Tell: at a ratio of 80 / 0.50 = 160, the strategy that lowers mortality is prone positioning, not an oscillatory mode.

D.q: A 38-year-old Black woman has a dry cough and dyspnea of insidious onset. She has lupus pernio (skin sores on the face), nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis brings an insidious dry cough with clubbing, inspiratory crackles and pleural-based honeycombing, and its no-biopsy rule applies over 65. Tell: skin sores and liver, spleen and node enlargement point to a multi-organ granulomatous disease.

Correct. Lupus pernio, skin sores on the face, is the skin involvement of sarcoidosis, and a dry cough, insidious dyspnea, nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement complete its multi-organ picture. Sarcoidosis also occurs more often in Black patients and in women.

Despite the shared word, lupus pernio is a sarcoidosis skin finding; systemic lupus erythematosus is a connective tissue cause of interstitial disease flagged by a high antinuclear antibody. Tell: facial sores with liver, spleen and node enlargement point to granulomas.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows organic dust exposure, with malaise, chills, fever and cough hours afterward. Tell: no exposure is described, and skin sores with liver, spleen and lymph node enlargement are multi-organ findings that dust does not explain.

D.q: In interstitial lung disease, what does a positive c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) test suggest?
opts: Correct. A positive c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, formerly Wegener's, a granulomatous vasculitis that is one of the interstitial lung diseases with a granulomatous response.

A high antinuclear antibody level points to collagen vascular disease; the cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody is a different test pointing elsewhere. Tell: antinuclear antibody for collagen vascular disease, cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody for granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Active sarcoidosis is suggested by an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and sarcoidosis can raise the angiotensin-converting enzyme level. Tell: sarcoidosis has its own laboratory markers, while the cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody points to polyangiitis.

Goodpasture syndrome is identified by antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies, and it combines glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Tell: basement membrane antibodies mean Goodpasture; the cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody means polyangiitis.

D.q: A 46-year-old woman who has never smoked has a small, flat nodular opacity lying along the minor fissure on computed tomography done after chest trauma. She asks whether it could be cancer. Which response is accurate?
opts: Removing it now treats a benign-looking opacity as cancer, yet a nodule close to a fissure usually indicates something benign and no concerning feature, such as a spiculated border, is described. Tell: an opacity hugging the minor fissure in a never-smoker is a typical benign finding.

This reverses the rule: a nodule close to a fissure usually indicates something benign. Tell: concerning locations are the upper lobes or hilar structures, and an opacity along the minor fissure is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue.

Correct. A nodule close to a fissure usually indicates something benign, and a nodular opacity adjacent to the minor fissure is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue. She is a never-smoker without other risk factors, which also lowers concern.

A hamartoma is a smoothly marginated solid nodule with internal fat and popcorn calcification. Tell: a flat opacity lying along the minor fissure, with no fat or calcification described, is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue.

D.q: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and a low albumin has had watery diarrhea for 6 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 36 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His albumin is 2.5 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). His anion gap calculates to 5. Which step comes next in interpreting the gap?
opts: Bromide intoxication is another rare cause of a low gap, kept for a gap that remains low once albumin is accounted for. His albumin is 2.5 g/dL and explains the low value. Tell: the common reason for a low gap is the albumin.

The raised-gap list is used when the gap is above 12. His measured gap is 5 and his corrected gap 10, both at or below normal, so the normal-gap list applies, and diarrhea is on it. Tell: correct first, then pick the list.
Screen for a plasma cell dyscrasia

Plasma cell dyscrasias lower the gap through cationic paraproteins, but they are considered only when the gap stays low after correction. His corrected gap is 10, normal. Tell: rule out the low albumin first.
Correct the gap for his low albumin

Correct. A low gap is most often a low albumin, and the gap must be corrected when albumin is abnormal. Adding 2.5 for each 1 g/dL below 4.5 gives 5 + 5 = 10, a normal gap, which fits a normal-gap metabolic acidosis from his diarrhea.

D.q: How many of Light's criteria must a pleural fluid meet to be classified as an exudate?
opts: Requiring all three describes the wrong side of the rule: a transudate is defined by all of Light's criteria being absent, and one present criterion makes an exudate. Tell: one met, exudate; none met, transudate.

Correct. An exudate meets at least one of Light's criteria: pleural-to-serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural-to-serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6, or pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase. A transudate meets none of them.

The protein ratio is one of the three criteria, but either lactate dehydrogenase criterion counts just as much. Tell: any single criterion, protein or lactate dehydrogenase, makes the fluid an exudate.
Requiring two criteria would misclassify exudates that meet a single one; any one criterion is enough. Tell: Light's criteria work as an 'any one' rule.

D.q: A 68-year-old man with a 50 pack-year history has a large, cavitated mass in the periphery of the left upper lobe. Weeks later he develops crampy abdominal pain, and imaging shows a metastasis in the small intestine. Biopsy of the lung mass shows undifferentiated cells about three times normal size that do not stain for mucin. Which lung cancer type is most likely?
opts: Adenocarcinoma is also peripheral, but it produces mucin, shown on a mucicarmine stain. Tell: his tumor cells are mucin-negative, very large and undifferentiated, and the cancer has reached the small intestine, an unusual site typical of large cell carcinoma.

Correct. Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery, shows a large cavitated mass on computed tomography, and has anaplastic, undifferentiated cells about 3 times larger than baseline that lack specific markers. Negative mucicarmine staining may point to it, and its spread to unusual sites such as the small intestine and bowel is characteristic.

Squamous cell carcinoma cavitates too, but it sits centrally and often arises in a bronchus. Tell: his mass is peripheral and has spread to the small intestine, a pattern specific to large cell carcinoma.
Small cell carcinoma is central, with small cells that lack nucleoli. Tell: his cells are about three times normal size and the mass is peripheral, the reverse of small cell features.

D.q: A 56-year-old coal miner has severe complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis with worsening dyspnea despite oxygen, vaccinations, pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking cessation. Which referral may be indicated?
opts: Correct. Management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis is supportive, with oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, and in severe cases lung transplant may be indicated. He has severe disease that is worsening despite every supportive measure on the list.

No effective curative treatment is available, and the listed management is supportive care with lung transplant for severe cases. Tell: removing the dust is not among the options described; replacing the lung is the step named for severe disease.

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a salvage option reserved for severe, refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: his disease is chronic dust-related fibrosis, for which the severe-case option is lung transplant, not acute salvage support.

Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation is part of sarcoidosis follow-up, to find and manage ocular inflammation. Tell: coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no eye monitoring step, and his severe, worsening lung disease points to transplant evaluation.
