E.q: A 71-year-old man with kidney failure has vomited for 3 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.39 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 39 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 92 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap, what is his change in anion gap?
opts: This is the change in bicarbonate, 25 - 23 = 2, not the change in gap. The change in gap is the calculated gap minus 10: 23 - 10 = 13. Tell: the two changes are compared with each other, so keep them apart.

Correct. Gap = 138 - (92 + 23) = 23. Change in gap = 23 - 10 = 13. Against a change in bicarbonate of only 25 - 23 = 2, the gap rose far more, the sign of a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting on top of the uremic acidosis.
This is the anion gap itself, 138 - (92 + 23). The change in gap subtracts the accepted normal of 10: 23 - 10 = 13. Tell: change in gap = calculated gap - 10.
This adds 10 to the gap instead of subtracting it. Change in gap = 23 - 10 = 13. Tell: the change is how far the gap has risen above 10.

E.io: Discuss screening tools for obstructive sleep apnea
E.q: A 56-year-old man is seen for evaluation before elective knee surgery and has no known sleep disorder. His wife says he snores loudly enough to be heard through closed doors and has seen him stop breathing during sleep. He denies daytime tiredness. He is treated for high blood pressure. His body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and his neck (shirt collar) measures 16.5 inches. What is his STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) score?
opts: A score of 4 drops two yes answers, such as age and neck: 56 is older than 50, and a 16.5-inch collar meets the 16-inch item. Tell: he meets three of the four Bang items (age, neck, male), on top of three yes answers to the first 4 questions (snoring, observed apnea, pressure).

A score of 5 misses one yes answer, most often the neck: the questionnaire counts a collar of 16 inches / 40 cm or larger for anyone, so 16.5 inches scores 1. Tell: on the questionnaire, the neck item has a single cut-off, 16 inches, whatever the patient's sex.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed apnea 1 + treated pressure 1 + body mass index 33 (not more than 35) 0 + age 56 (older than 50) 1 + neck 16.5 inches (16 or larger) 1 + male 1 = 6. A score of 5 to 8 places him in the high-risk group for obstructive sleep apnea before his surgery.

A score of 7 adds a point for body mass index, but the item asks for more than 35 kg/m2, and his 33 does not qualify. Tell: being obese is not enough for the B item; it needs a body mass index above 35, and his tiredness item is also a no.

E.q: A 44-year-old woman has interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern. She has no occupational exposures, takes no medicines and has no hilar adenopathy. Her clinician wants a laboratory test that screens for a collagen vascular disease as the cause. Which test fits?
opts: Correct. A high antinuclear antibody points to the collagen vascular diseases, the connective tissue disorders such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome and systemic sclerosis that produce an inflammatory, fibrotic interstitial response. With no exposures or drugs, an autoimmune cause is the next to consider.

Antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies identify Goodpasture syndrome, with glomerulonephritis and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in young adults. Tell: she has no hemorrhage or kidney findings, and the collagen vascular screen is the antinuclear antibody.

An elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is seen in 40-80% of patients with sarcoidosis. Tell: she has no hilar adenopathy to suggest sarcoidosis, and the test for collagen vascular disease is the antinuclear antibody.

A positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a granulomatous vasculitis. Tell: the clinician wants a collagen vascular screen, and the test paired with collagen vascular disease is the antinuclear antibody.

E.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
E.q: Carbon dioxide rises from 40 to 70 mm Hg within the past hour, from a baseline bicarbonate of 24 mEq/L. The acute bicarbonate rise is 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg and the chronic rise is 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg. What bicarbonate is expected?
opts: 24 mEq/L assumes no compensation at all, but even acutely plasma bicarbonate rises 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg through cell buffering. A 30 mm Hg rise adds 3, giving 27. Tell: acute compensation is small, not zero.
Correct. A rise within the past hour is acute, so bicarbonate climbs 1 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg. Carbon dioxide rose 30 mm Hg, three steps of 10, so bicarbonate rises 3: 24 + 3 = 27 mEq/L.

30 mEq/L uses 2 per 10 mm Hg, the acute respiratory alkalosis ratio. Acute respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate 1 per 10 mm Hg: 3 steps add 3, giving 27. Tell: use the ratio for the disorder in front of you.

34.5 mEq/L applies the chronic ratio, 3.5 per 10 mm Hg, which needs 24 to 48 hours of sustained raised carbon dioxide. A rise within the past hour is acute, 1 per 10, giving 27. Tell: the kidneys have not had days to act.

E.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
E.q: A 67-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has had nasogastric suction for 3 days after bowel surgery. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.41 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide. What does his bicarbonate indicate?
opts: Acute compensation adds only 1 per 10 mm Hg, predicting 25 + 2 = 27, far below his 37, and his lung disease is long-standing. Tell: the acute ratio fits a sudden rise over hours; it cannot explain a bicarbonate of 37.

A concurrent metabolic acidosis would hold bicarbonate below the predicted 32. His is 37, above it. Tell: bicarbonate above prediction means metabolic alkalosis; below prediction means metabolic acidosis.

Correct. Chronic compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 3.5 x (60 - 40) / 10 = 25 + 7 = 32. His is 37, 5 above prediction, so something beyond the kidneys is adding bicarbonate: loss of gastric acid by suction. A normal pH with a high carbon dioxide also signals a mixed disorder.

Appropriate chronic compensation would give a bicarbonate near 32, and compensation alone never returns the pH to a normal 7.41. His 37 overshoots. Tell: a bicarbonate above the chronic prediction adds a metabolic alkalosis.

E.q: A 48-year-old man has worked as a sandblaster for 20 years. He has dyspnea, cough, weight loss and fatigue with crackles on examination. His chest film shows nodular opacities, 1-10 mm across, throughout both lungs, and eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sarcoidosis also enlarges the hilar nodes, with symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy. Tell: twenty years of sandblasting and eggshell calcification of the nodes point to silica, and his history, not the film alone, names the disease.

Correct. Sandblasting is a free crystalline silica exposure, and silicosis shows silicotic nodules 1-10 mm across throughout the lungs with eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. Dyspnea, cough, weight loss, fatigue and crackles fit its presentation.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows organic dust and shows small nodular densities sparing the apices and the bases. Tell: sand is inorganic silica, and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes belongs to silicosis.

Asbestosis follows insulation, demolition, shipyard or construction work and shows pleural plaques with streaking at the bases. Tell: his exposure is silica sand, and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes is a silicosis sign.

E.q: A 45-year-old woman who has never smoked and has no family history of lung cancer has a solitary 4-mm solid nodule found on computed tomography done for abdominal pain. She asks whether she should be worried about it. Which response is accurate?
opts: Correct. The first evaluation of a nodule is its size, and anything smaller than 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is at high risk. Most nodules are benign, mainly granulomas or hamartomas. She has no smoking or family history, so her 4-mm nodule falls in the low-concern group.

A biopsy is not the step for a nodule this small in a low-risk patient: anything smaller than 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is at high risk. Tell: biopsy belongs to concerning nodules, such as those with intense uptake or a high probability of malignancy.

Size is the first thing assessed, and 6 mm is the threshold: smaller nodules are generally not concerning, while nodules greater than 6 mm raise concern. Tell: her 4-mm nodule sits below that line in a patient without risk factors.

Most lung nodules are benign, mainly granulomas (inflammatory) or hamartomas (connective tissue growth). Tell: concern rises with size above 6 mm, upper lobe or hilar location, a spiky border or a high-risk patient, and her nodule has none of these.

E.topic: Metabolic acidosis: causes and the anion gap
E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 72-year-old man has chronic kidney failure that has worsened over months, adrenal insufficiency on hormone replacement, glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, and leg edema treated with a loop diuretic. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. His bicarbonate is 15 and his pH 7.32. Tell: a diuretic pushes the pH the other way.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause a normal-gap acidosis by bicarbonate loss. His gap is 20. Tell: a raised gap needs unmeasured anions, which failing kidneys retain.
Adrenal insufficiency causes a normal-gap acidosis, with a gap of 6 to 12 and a high chloride. His gap is 20 and his chloride 103. Tell: adrenal insufficiency is on the normal-gap list.

Correct. Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 138 - (15 + 103) = 20, above 12. Renal failure, acute or chronic, is one of the big four raised-gap causes. His other conditions do not raise the gap.

E.topic: Metabolic acidosis: Winter formula and the change in anion gap
E.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
E.q: What does the Winter formula predict?
opts: Correct. The Winter formula, expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x bicarbonate + 8 plus or minus 2, predicts the respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, raised gap or normal gap. Carbon dioxide above the range means a concurrent respiratory acidosis; below means a concurrent respiratory alkalosis.
In metabolic alkalosis the carbon dioxide rises about 0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate; that is a separate rule. Tell: the Winter formula is for metabolic acidosis.
The gap is corrected by adding 2.5 for each 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4.5. Tell: the Winter formula predicts the carbon dioxide, not the gap.

Bicarbonate in respiratory acidosis is predicted from the carbon dioxide rise: 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg acutely, 3.5 chronically. Tell: the Winter formula starts from the bicarbonate and predicts the carbon dioxide.

E.q: A 61-year-old woman received chest radiation for breast cancer 3 years ago. She now has interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern and has no occupational exposures. She asks whether her cancer treatment could be the cause. Which response is accurate?
opts: No, cancer treatment spares the lungs

Cancer treatment does not spare the lungs: both radiation and chemotherapeutics are treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease. Tell: her treatment history is part of the cause search, and her chest radiation stands out in it.
No, radiation affects the skin alone

Radiation reaches more than the skin: it is a treatment-related cause of interstitial lung disease and is listed among causes with an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response. Tell: her past chest radiation is a recognized cause of exactly this lung disease.
Yes, by acting as an inhaled dust

Inhaled inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes make up the occupational and environmental group, as in silicosis or farmer's lung. Tell: radiation belongs to the treatment-related group, not to the inhaled exposures, so the mechanism offered is wrong.
Yes, radiation is a recognized cause

Correct. Radiation is one of the treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease of known cause, listed with methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics. It is also named among the causes that provoke an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response, so her chest radiation is a credible cause.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
E.q: A 52-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated events in which thermistor airflow falls by 90% or more for 15 seconds while chest and abdominal respiratory effort continue. How is each event classified?
opts: Correct. An apnea is a 90% or greater fall in airflow on the thermistor lasting at least 10 seconds, and when airflow stops but respiratory effort continues, the apnea is obstructive. The airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe, the event pattern of obstructive sleep apnea.

A mixed apnea opens with no respiratory effort, and effort resumes only during the latter part of the event. Tell: his effort is present from the start of each event to its end, which is the obstructive pattern rather than the mixed one.

A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, short of a near-total stop. Tell: a fall in airflow of 90% or more is near or total cessation of breathing, which defines an apnea.

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops sending the signal to breathe. Tell: his chest and abdomen keep moving throughout each event, so effort is present and the event is not central.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
E.q: A 34-year-old woman lies in bed at lights-out with her eyes closed. Her electroencephalogram shows rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, strongest over the occipital region. Which state does this tracing represent?
opts: Stage N1 is the drowsy transition into light sleep, and its tracing has slowed to theta waves. Tell: a steady, rhythmical 8 to 13 per second over the occipital region is alpha, so she is still awake and resting.

Rapid eye movement sleep shows an irregular, mixed, low-voltage, beta-like tracing with sawtooth waves. Tell: rhythmical alpha at lights-out with closed eyes is quiet wakefulness, well before the first rapid eye movement period about 90 minutes in.

Alert wakefulness, with the eyes open and the person alert and active, shows beta waves faster than 14 cycles per second. Tell: a rhythmical 8 to 13 per second with the eyes closed is alpha, the relaxed waking state.

Correct. Rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, strongest over the occipital region, are alpha waves, the mark of quiet wakefulness: an awake person with the eyes closed, relaxed, with a decreased level of alertness. She has not yet fallen asleep.

E.q: In which stage of small cell carcinoma does radiation work best?
opts: Extensive stage has spread away from the local area. Tell: radiation works best while the disease is confined, in limited stage.
Radiation does not work equally at every stage; it works best in limited stage, confined to one area with local lymph nodes involved. Tell: the more confined the disease, the better radiation works.

Combined small cell carcinoma means different histological types mixed with non-small cell cancer, and it is not the category named for the best radiation response. Tell: radiation works best in limited stage, confined to one area with only local lymph nodes involved.

Correct. Small cell carcinoma is divided by metastasis into limited stage, confined to one area with only local lymph nodes involved, extensive stage, spread away from the local area, and combined. Radiation works best when the cancer is in limited stage.

E.q: A 58-year-old woman in the intensive care unit has a subclavian vein catheter placed for venous access. An hour later she reports new right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, and a chest radiograph shows a visceral pleural line on the right. She has no history of lung disease or chest trauma. How is her pneumothorax classified?
opts: Traumatic pneumothorax follows blunt or penetrating trauma to the thorax, such as a gunshot or stab wound. Tell: a needle placed during a procedure makes this iatrogenic, the category for pleural injury caused by a medical intervention.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax arises with no thoracic trauma and no underlying lung abnormality, classically in tall, thin young males. Tell: hers followed a procedure, so it is not spontaneous at all.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Iatrogenic pneumothorax is injury to the pleura secondary to a medical intervention, and subclavian vein catheter placement is one of the listed examples, with thoracentesis, bronchoscopy and mechanical ventilation. Her symptoms began an hour after the catheter, with no lung disease or trauma.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax needs an underlying lung abnormality, most commonly chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Tell: she has no lung disease, and the timing ties the event to the catheter placement.
ruled out by a stated finding

Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
E.q: A 59-year-old man who smokes has a bronchial biopsy showing dysplasia: the cells have changed form but have not invaded the surrounding tissue. He asks what would come next if these cells keep progressing. Which change comes next?
opts: Invasion of normal tissue with entry into blood and lymph marks a malignant tumor, which follows in situ cancer rather than dysplasia directly. Tell: in situ cancer, cells that stay in one place, sits between dysplasia and invasion.

Hyperplasia, cells dividing more rapidly than normal, comes before dysplasia in the sequence, not after it. Tell: his cells have already changed form, which is dysplasia, so the next stage is in situ cancer, cells that stay in one place.

Correct. Lung cancer develops in a sequence: a genetically altered epithelial cell, hyperplasia (cells dividing faster than normal), dysplasia (cells changing form), in situ cancer (cells staying in one place), then a malignant tumor whose cells invade normal tissue and enter blood and lymph, and finally distant metastases. After dysplasia comes in situ cancer.

Metastases at distant sites are the last stage of the sequence, after in situ cancer and invasion into blood and lymph. Tell: his biopsy shows dysplasia without invasion, so two stages still separate him from distant spread.

Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
E.q: What is the most common presenting symptom of interstitial lung disease?
opts: The cough of interstitial lung disease is persistent and nonproductive, not productive, and even so it is less common than breathlessness as the presenting complaint. Tell: a dry cough fits scarred, stiff lung tissue; dyspnea is the most common presentation.

Hemoptysis is on the list of presenting symptoms but is not the common one; stiff, restrictive lungs make shortness of breath the usual complaint. Tell: hemoptysis is a listed but less usual symptom, while progressive exertional dyspnea leads.

Correct. Fibrosis makes the lung tissue stiff and restrictive, no longer expanding as it once did, which makes breathing harder; patients most commonly present with shortness of breath, typically progressive exertional dyspnea, sometimes with a persistent nonproductive cough.

Chest pain can occur in interstitial lung disease but is a less usual complaint than dyspnea. Lung that cannot expand is what makes breathing hard. Tell: the leading complaint follows from the restrictive physiology, which is breathlessness, first on exertion and later at rest.

E.q: A 66-year-old man with a 3.5-cm non-small cell lung carcinoma, no lymph node involvement and no metastasis (stage 1B) is fit for surgery. He would prefer to avoid an operation and asks for chemotherapy and radiation instead. Which plan should be avoided as his primary treatment?
opts: Correct. Stage 1 non-small cell lung cancer is treated with surgical resection when the patient can tolerate it, and chemotherapy and radiation serve only as adjuncts to surgery or for stage 4, because non-small cell cancers respond poorly to them. For a fit patient with stage 1B disease, replacing surgery with chemoradiation gives up the standard treatment.

Wedge or segment resection, removing a smaller or larger portion of the lobe, is a standard resection chosen by size and lymph involvement. Tell: resection is the recommended treatment for his stage, so it is appropriate.

Pulmonary function tests are part of the workup, and a patient must be able to tolerate surgery, surviving and recovering from it. Tell: checking his lung function before resection supports the standard plan rather than conflicting with it.
Lobectomy, removing the entire lobe, is one of the standard resections for stage 1 disease in a patient who can tolerate surgery. Tell: he is fit, so this is the treatment to pursue, not to avoid.

E.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
E.q: A 2-month-old boy's electroencephalogram shows slow waves below 3.5 cycles per second. Compared with most other types of brain waves, how large is their voltage expected to be?
opts: Low voltage describes beta waves, the asynchronous, fast waves of an alert, actively thinking person, not delta waves. Tell: slow delta waves are the tall ones, often 2 to 4 times the voltage of most other brain waves.

Delta waves stand out by their size: their voltage is often 2 to 4 times greater than that of most other brain waves. Tell: on traces drawn to one voltage scale, the delta trace rises well above the alpha, beta and theta traces.

Correct. Delta waves, which include all waves below 3.5 cycles per second and occur in infancy, often have voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other types of brain waves. On a tracing they stand out as tall, slow waves, in contrast to the low-voltage beta waves of an alert adult.

This overstates the difference tenfold: delta waves are often 2 to 4 times greater in voltage than most other brain waves. Tell: the multiplier to remember is 2 to 4, not tens of times, for these slow waves of infancy and deep sleep.

Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
E.q: Which central lung cancer is usually metastatic by the time it is diagnosed?
opts: Correct. Small cell carcinoma is central, infiltrates the mucosa and develops insidiously, so over 70% of patients are already metastatic to the liver, bone or brain before detection. That is why it is usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis.

Squamous cell carcinoma is central too, but it is the type that can be caught with sputum testing, and it spreads by local invasion and lymphangitic spread to hilar nodes. Tell: central and metastatic at diagnosis points to small cell.
Adenocarcinoma is peripheral, found in the mid-lung and periphery, so it does not fit a central tumor. Tell: the central type that is usually metastatic at diagnosis is small cell.
ruled out by a stated finding

Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery and metastasizes to unusual sites such as the small intestine and bowel. Tell: a central location rules it out; small cell is central and usually metastatic at diagnosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.q: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history has sudden sharp left chest pain that worsens with deep breathing. Before the pain is attributed to pleurisy, which condition belongs among those that must be considered immediately?
opts: Costochondritis, inflammation of the costal cartilage, belongs to the second group, the other causes to consider. Tell: it is not one of the dangerous conditions weighed first, which are myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism.

Nerve root pain from herpes zoster is another of the other causes to consider once the dangerous ones are excluded. Tell: the immediate list is myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism.

Rib fracture is listed with the other causes of chest pain, after the dangerous ones. Tell: the conditions that must be considered immediately are the dangerous ones, and aortic dissection is on that list.

Correct. Pleuritic pain demands immediate consideration of the dangerous causes: myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism. Only after those are weighed are the other causes, such as rib fracture, costochondritis, vertebral fracture or zoster nerve pain, considered.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. E.q: A 74-year-old woman has a very large left pleural effusion, estimated at more than 1,000 mL on imaging, with marked dyspnea. Which inspection finding is expected?
opts: A large effusion pushes the trachea away from the involved side, not toward it; that shift appears once the fluid passes 1,000 mL. Tell: her fluid is on the left, so the shift is to the right.
Inspection over a pleural effusion shows asymmetrical thoracic expansion, the affected side moving less. Tell: a left effusion over 1,000 mL limits expansion on that side.

Correct. With an effusion over 1,000 mL, the trachea shifts away from the involved side, so a left effusion pushes it to the right; inspection also shows asymmetrical thoracic expansion. Small effusions under 300 mL produce no examination findings, but hers is large.
Small effusions, under 300 mL, produce no physical examination findings. Tell: hers is more than 1,000 mL, large enough to shift the trachea away from the effusion.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
E.q: Which apex-to-cupola distance separates a small from a large pneumothorax in the American College of Chest Physicians system?
opts: One centimeter is the size that separates a bleb, under 1 cm, from a bulla, over 1 cm, not a small from a large pneumothorax. Tell: pneumothorax size uses the 3 cm apex-to-cupola line.

Two centimeters is not the threshold in this system; the apex-to-cupola cutoff is 3 cm. Tell: one number for size, 3 cm at the apex, sorts observation from chest tube in a symptomatic primary pneumothorax.

Correct. The American College of Chest Physicians defines pneumothorax size by the apex-to-cupola distance, with a distance under 3 cm called small and larger distances called large. That one number then sorts the treatment of primary and secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.

Five centimeters would label many large pneumothoraces small; the American College of Chest Physicians line is drawn at 3 cm from apex to cupola. Tell: a primary pneumothorax beyond 3 cm with moderate or severe symptoms already needs a chest tube.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
E.q: A 34-year-old man on a mountain trek at high altitude wakes frequently at night. His tent partner notices that his breathing speeds up and then stops, over and over, without snoring. He has no heart failure and takes no medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Nocturnal asthma is on the differential for nighttime breathing complaints. Tell: the cycle of hyperventilation alternating with apnea, at high altitude, matches both the risk factor and the mechanism of central sleep apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea comes from upper airway narrowing and usually brings loud, habitual snoring. Tell: a repeating cycle of fast breathing and then no breathing, at altitude and without snoring, is the central pattern.

Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings. Tell: a repeating cycle of hyperventilation and apnea during sleep at high altitude is the breathing pattern of central apnea, not an anxiety episode.

Correct. High altitude is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, in which increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide produces an unstable pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea. Frequent awakenings without snoring fit, since snoring is less common than in obstructive sleep apnea.

E.topic: Pleural effusion: imaging and fluid analysis
E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
E.q: A 62-year-old woman with a new pleural effusion undergoes diagnostic thoracentesis. Pleural fluid protein is 3.9 g/dL with serum protein 6.5 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 150 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 200 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). How many of Light's criteria does the fluid meet, and what does that make it?
opts: A transudate needs every criterion absent. Tell: her protein ratio, 3.9 / 6.5 = 0.60, and her lactate dehydrogenase ratio, 150 / 200 = 0.75, both cross their cutoffs.

Exudate is right, but the count misses a criterion. Tell: both ratios are met, protein 0.60 above 0.5 and lactate dehydrogenase 0.75 above 0.6; only the level criterion, 150 against about 187, is not.

Correct. Protein ratio 3.9 / 6.5 = 0.60, above 0.5: met. Lactate dehydrogenase ratio 150 / 200 = 0.75, above 0.6: met. Fluid lactate dehydrogenase 150 is under two-thirds of the 280 upper limit, about 187: not met. Two of three, and one is already enough for an exudate.
Exudate is right, but the third criterion is not met. Tell: fluid lactate dehydrogenase of 150 is under two-thirds of the 280 upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase, about 187.

E.q: A 66-year-old retired construction worker has asbestosis with exertional dyspnea and fine bibasilar crackles. He asks about a procedure to wash the asbestos fibers out of his lungs. Which treatment plan fits?
opts: Lavage to wash out the fibers

Asbestos fibers cannot be removed from lung tissue once they invade it, which is why treatment is supportive. Tell: bronchoalveolar lavage is a diagnostic study, used in silicosis to show milky fluid, not a way to clear asbestos.

Methotrexate is a corticosteroid alternative in sarcoidosis and is itself implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: asbestosis treatment is supportive: oxygen therapy, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations.

The fibers cannot be removed by any means, and the fibrosis they cause is permanent scar tissue. Tell: corticosteroids appear in the plans for sarcoidosis and severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis, while asbestosis care is supportive.

Correct. Treatment of asbestosis is supportive because asbestos fibers invade lung tissue and cannot be removed. Oxygen therapy, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations make up that care, while the scarring itself comes from chronic inflammation and macrophage invasion forming fibrosis.

Acute respiratory disease syndrome (ARDS)
E.q: Which finding gives a definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
opts: Chest radiograph and computed tomography show little change acutely, with fibrotic changes only in subacute and chronic disease, so a normal-looking film cannot define the diagnosis. Tell: imaging lags; antibodies to the agent confirm.

Correct. Antibodies to the agent in serum give a definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Supporting findings include an elevated white blood cell count with a left shift, hypoxia and restrictive pulmonary function, and lung biopsy may be indicated in subacute or chronic disease.

Restrictive dysfunction is common to many interstitial lung diseases, from idiopathic fibrosis to asbestosis, so it cannot single out hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: restriction is shared, while antibodies to the agent are specific.
White cell count with left shift

An elevated white blood cell count with a left shift supports the diagnosis but does not identify the antigen, so it is not definitive. Tell: inflammation markers support; antibodies to the specific agent define.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
E.q: A 54-year-old woman collapses 6 days after a cesarean delivery. She is pale and sweating, her heart rate is 128/min, her blood pressure is 78/48 mmHg and her neck veins are distended. Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography shows a large central pulmonary embolism, and echocardiography shows an acutely dilated right ventricle with the septum bowing toward the left ventricle. What best explains her hypotension?
opts: Hypertrophy is the slow, compensatory response to chronic pressure from lung disease over months to years. Tell: her failure came within hours of a massive embolism, and acute pressure gives sudden dilation, not a thickened wall.

Correct. A massive embolism spikes right ventricular wall tension, and the right ventricle dilates acutely. The septum bows leftward into the left ventricle, so left ventricular diastolic filling falls, output plummets and systemic hypotension follows. Her distended neck veins and septal shift trace that chain.

Her left ventricle is squeezed from outside, not weakened: the problem is filling, because the bowed septum leaves the left ventricle less room in diastole. Tell: the echocardiogram shows the septum shifting toward the left ventricle, which limits filling rather than contraction.

Systemic vasodilation with an endothelial leak is the picture of sepsis, without right ventricular strain. Tell: she has distended neck veins, an acutely dilated right ventricle and a large central embolism, an obstructive cause of shock.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
E.q: A 67-year-old man has a biopsy-proven 2.5-cm non-small cell carcinoma in the left upper lobe. Positron emission tomography shows uptake in mediastinal and subcarinal lymph nodes on the same side as the tumor, and there is no distant metastasis. Which stage is his cancer?
opts: Stage 2B with a small tumor allows spread only to peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes. Tell: his nodes are mediastinal and subcarinal, N2, which pushes any cancer into stage 3.

Correct. Mediastinal or subcarinal node involvement (N2) automatically moves a cancer to stage 3, and a tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the mediastinal and subcarinal nodes is stage 3A. His tumor is only 2.5 cm, but the same-side mediastinal nodes set the stage.

Stage 3B with a tumor of 5 cm or less needs mediastinal or hilar nodes on the side without the tumor, or supraclavicular or scalene nodes. Tell: his nodes are on the same side as a 2.5-cm tumor, which is stage 3A.

Stage 4A needs spread to the other lung, the pleura or pericardium, the fluid around the lungs or heart, or one site outside the chest. Tell: he has no distant metastasis, and every stage 1 to 3 cancer is M0.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis takes a diuretic, is anxious and has low albumin. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.58 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 34 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 31 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 135 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 93 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in metabolic alkalosis carbon dioxide rises 0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate. Which part of her history best explains the metabolic alkalosis?
opts: Correct. Bicarbonate 31 with pH 7.58 is a metabolic alkalosis; expected carbon dioxide = 40 + 0.75 x 6 = 44.5, but hers is 34, so a respiratory alkalosis is also present. Diuretics are a saline-responsive cause of metabolic alkalosis, and liver disease with diuretics is the listed setting.

Liver disease is part of the listed setting, but the cause of metabolic alkalosis in that pair is the diuretic, which drives sodium reabsorption with hydrogen secretion. Tell: look for a listed alkalosis cause, such as a diuretic, vomiting or suction.
Low albumin lowers the measured anion gap and calls for correcting it; it is not a listed cause of metabolic alkalosis. Tell: low albumin changes the gap calculation.

Anxiety causes hyperventilation and explains the respiratory alkalosis, the low carbon dioxide of 34. It does not raise bicarbonate. Tell: the metabolic side needs a bicarbonate-raising cause, the diuretic.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary vascular disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
E.q: Which activity advice fits an adult with pulmonary hypertension?
opts: The exercise advised is regular, steady aerobic activity in a supervised rehabilitation program, not bursts of maximal effort on one's own. Tell: steady and supervised are the two key words.

Correct. Strict bedrest is avoided: regular, steady aerobic exercise in a supervised rehabilitation program is safe, prevents muscle deconditioning and improves fatigue. It sits alongside careful diuresis, oxygen during sleep or exertion and annual influenza and pneumococcal immunization.
Strict bedrest is specifically avoided in pulmonary hypertension because inactivity feeds muscle deconditioning. Tell: the advice is supervised, steady aerobic exercise, not rest.

Waiting for fatigue to pass invites deconditioning, and supervised aerobic exercise is what improves fatigue in pulmonary hypertension. Tell: activity is part of the treatment, not something to postpone.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
E.q: A 63-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension has ankle edema, ascites and a right ventricular S3 gallop. Her symptoms have worsened rapidly over 3 months, she has fainted several times, she is short of breath at rest (World Health Organization functional class IV), and her six-minute walk distance is 140 m. Which prognostic risk band fits her?
opts: Low risk needs no failure signs, slow progression, no syncope, class I or II and a walk above 440 m. Tell: she has every high-risk feature, starting with signs of right ventricular failure.
Intermediate risk has no right ventricular failure signs, occasional syncope, class III and a walk of 165-440 m. Tell: she has failure signs, repeated faints, class IV symptoms and a 140 m walk.
High is the right band, but 5-10% is the estimated 1-year mortality of the intermediate group. Tell: the high-risk group carries more than 10%.

Correct. Signs of right ventricular failure (edema, ascites, a right ventricular S3) place her in the high-risk row, and every other feature agrees: rapid progression, repeated syncope, class IV and a walk under 165 m. High risk carries an estimated 1-year mortality above 10%.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
E.q: With 5 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour of sleep, what else confirms obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Serum bicarbonate above 27 raises the chance of obesity hypoventilation syndrome and calls for an arterial blood gas; it plays no part in confirming obstructive apnea. Tell: bicarbonate screens for hypoventilation, not obstruction.

A screening questionnaire estimates risk, mainly in symptomatic patients in high-risk settings such as preoperative evaluation; it cannot confirm the diagnosis. Tell: confirmation needs events on a sleep study plus a qualifying symptom.

A body mass index above 30 is the obesity criterion for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Obesity is a risk factor for obstructive apnea but does not complete its diagnostic criterion. Tell: the pairing at 5 events per hour is events plus a symptom.

Correct. At 5 or more events per hour, one qualifying symptom completes the diagnosis: sleepiness, fatigue or insomnia impairing quality of life; waking with breath holding, gasping or choking; or habitual snoring or breathing interruptions noted by an observer.
E.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 16, 32

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary nodules and neoplasms in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
E.q: A 67-year-old woman smoked 2 packs a day for 20 years and quit 8 years ago. She has no cough, hemoptysis or weight loss, and no lung nodule has ever been found. She asks about lung cancer screening. Which is the most appropriate recommendation?
opts: Correct. Screening is recommended for high-risk adults without symptoms or a known nodule who are 55 to 80 years old, with at least a 30 pack-year history, who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years. She is 67, has 2 packs a day x 20 years = 40 pack-years, and quit 8 years ago, so she qualifies for an annual low-dose chest scan.

Sputum cytology is not sensitive and is not the screening test. Tell: eligible patients are screened annually with low-dose chest computed tomography, which works because air and nodules contrast sharply.
Quitting does not disqualify her: people who quit within the last 15 years still qualify. Tell: she quit 8 years ago, at 67 years old with 40 pack-years, so she meets every screening criterion.

Screening uses a lower radiation dose than a standard chest scan to reduce radiation exposure, which works because lung tissue gives high contrast between air and nodules. Tell: the screening study is the low-dose scan, not a standard-dose one.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
E.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after a high-speed motor vehicle crash. He is in severe respiratory distress, with blood pressure 78/50 mm Hg and heart rate 136 beats per minute. His trachea is deviated to the left, his neck veins are distended, his right chest is hyperresonant and breath sounds are absent on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hemothorax is blood in the pleural space, and fluid is dull to percussion. Tell: his right chest is hyperresonant, the note of air, and his trachea is pushed away from it under pressure.
ruled out by a stated finding

An open pneumothorax needs a direct wound in the chest wall that lets air in during inhalation. Tell: no chest wall wound is described, and his shock with tracheal shift marks trapped air under tension.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Air enters the pleural space but cannot escape, a one-way valve, causing severe ventilatory compromise and a mediastinal shift to the contralateral side. Decreased venous return and cardiac output follow, with hypotension, tracheal deviation, neck vein distention and absent breath sounds, his exact picture.

Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinal tissues, found as subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and a crunch with each heartbeat. Tell: his findings are a hyperresonant, silent hemithorax with shock and tracheal shift.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for pulmonary vascular disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 7. adult 8. elderly
E.q: An 84-year-old woman with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is admitted with acute pulmonary edema. Her blood pressure is 148/82 mmHg and her creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.1). Echocardiography shows a stiff, thick left ventricle with a high end-diastolic pressure. Which diuresis strategy fits her?
opts: Under-diuresis leaves the lungs flooded and brings recurrent pulmonary edema. Tell: she needs fluid removed, just carefully; her margin is narrow on both sides.

Correct. Elderly patients usually have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction from age-related myocardial stiffening, with a high end-diastolic pressure and extreme sensitivity to preload. Their therapeutic margin is narrow, so diuresis must be gentle and precise.

Aggressive diuresis is generally well tolerated by younger adults with reduced ejection fraction and more physiological reserve. Tell: in her stiff, preload-dependent ventricle, over-diuresis causes precipitous hypotension.

Morphine is a use-with-caution agent in the toolbox, because it risks respiratory depression, and it does not replace diuresis. Tell: her problem is the pace of fluid removal in a preload-sensitive heart.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
E.q: Needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax is also known as what?
opts: Tube thoracostomy is chest tube placement to drain fluid or air, the step that follows needle decompression. Tell: needle thoracostomy is the temporary needle; tube thoracostomy is the chest tube.

Correct. Needle decompression, also known as needle thoracostomy, is insertion of a needle into the pleural space to decompress a tension pneumothorax, typically in the 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, at the midclavicular line.

Catheter aspiration uses a large-gauge needle on a catheter with a stopcock and syringe for a small primary pneumothorax, and tension is a contraindication to it. Tell: same landmark, different procedure and different patient.
Thoracentesis removes pleural fluid, diagnostically or therapeutically, from an effusion. Tell: thoracentesis is for fluid; decompressing trapped air in tension is a needle thoracostomy.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
E.q: A 51-year-old woman has sudden dyspnea and a swollen, tender left leg, and her Wells score is 6. She had anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast during a previous scan. Her creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.1), and she has no chronic lung disease. Which test should confirm or exclude pulmonary embolism?
opts: A D-dimer is bypassed when the Wells score is above 4, because a likely embolism needs imaging. Tell: at 6 she goes straight to imaging, and her allergy decides which kind.

Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography is the modern first-line test, but it depends on intravenous iodinated contrast. Tell: her anaphylaxis to that contrast is a severe allergy, so the perfusion scan is the choice.
ruled out by a stated finding
Echocardiography has poor sensitivity (about 50%) for acute embolism and is used for risk stratification, not diagnosis. Tell: it can show right ventricular strain but cannot exclude embolism.

Correct. Severe contrast allergy is one of the reasons to choose the ventilation-perfusion scan over computed tomographic pulmonary angiography. With no chronic lung disease the scan is less likely to be nondiagnostic, and a completely negative scan excludes embolism with the same certainty as a negative pulmonary angiogram.

E.topic: Normal values and the anion gap
E.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure, poor tissue perfusion and a low albumin is admitted. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 32 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 108 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His albumin is 2.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). What is his anion gap after correction for his albumin?
opts: This is the uncorrected gap, 140 - (16 + 108) = 16. With an albumin of 2.9 g/dL the gap must be corrected upward by 4. Tell: a low albumin makes the measured gap read too low.
This counts the albumin drop from 3.5, the bottom of the normal range: (3.5 - 2.9) x 2.5 = 1.5. The correction counts from 4.5 g/dL, a 1.6 g/dL drop worth 4. Tell: start the correction at 4.5.

Correct. The measured gap is 140 - (16 + 108) = 16. His albumin is 4.5 - 2.9 = 1.6 g/dL below 4.5, and 1.6 x 2.5 = 4, so the corrected gap is 16 + 4 = 20, a raised gap that fits lactic acidosis from poor perfusion.
This counts the albumin drop from 5.5, the top of the normal range: (5.5 - 2.9) x 2.5 = 6.5. The correction counts from 4.5 g/dL, a 1.6 g/dL drop worth 4. Tell: start the correction at 4.5.

E.topic: Pulmonary embolism: risk stratification and treatment
E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
E.q: A 44-year-old man has a small pulmonary embolism on computed tomographic pulmonary angiography, with a normal right ventricle. His blood pressure is 132/84 mmHg, his troponin I is under 0.01 ng/mL (normal under 0.04), and his B-type natriuretic peptide is 40 pg/mL (normal under 100). How is his embolism risk-stratified, and what follows for treatment?
opts: Correct. Normotension, no right ventricular dysfunction and negative cardiac biomarkers define low-risk embolism. It carries an excellent prognosis and is treated with standard anticoagulation, which halts clot propagation while the body's own fibrinolysis works.
Every confirmed embolism is anticoagulated at once, low risk included. Tell: the goal is to halt clot propagation and allow endogenous fibrinolysis, which needs treatment.
Massive embolism means sustained hypotension, pulselessness or profound bradycardia. Tell: his blood pressure is 132/84 mmHg, and thrombolysis would add bleeding risk for no gain.

Submassive embolism needs right ventricular dysfunction on echocardiography or computed tomography, or a raised troponin or natriuretic peptide. Tell: his right ventricle and both biomarkers are normal.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for pleural disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 2. adult 3. elderly
E.q: A 78-year-old woman with known heart failure has increasing lower extremity edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and her chest radiograph shows bilateral pleural effusions. She is comfortable at rest. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Her edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea give the effusions a clear clinical cause: heart failure, which raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes more than 90% of transudates. Effusions are managed by treating the underlying disorder, and diuretics are the initial treatment for heart failure transudates.
Pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space and is often used for recurrent malignant effusions as palliative care. Tell: her effusions come from heart failure, treated by treating the heart failure.
Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed for a new pleural effusion with no clinical cause. Tell: her heart failure story explains the bilateral effusions, so treating the cause comes first.
ruled out by a stated finding

An indwelling tunneled pleural catheter suits a non-expandable lung, rapidly recurring fluid or a short prognosis. Tell: she is comfortable, and her effusions should respond to treating the heart failure.

E.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
E.q: A 30-year-old resident falls asleep after a 30-hour shift without any sleep. What is expected of the rapid eye movement episodes on her recording tonight?
opts: Correct. When a person is extremely sleepy, each rapid eye movement episode is short or even absent; as the person becomes more rested, the episodes lengthen. After 30 hours awake she is extremely sleepy, so tonight her rapid eye movement episodes should be brief or missing.
The same as on rested nights

Episode length is not fixed; it depends on how sleepy the person is. Tell: extreme sleepiness makes each rapid eye movement episode short or even absent, so her recording should look different from a rested night's.

Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes within 90- to 120-minute cycles, and extreme sleepiness changes their length, making each one short or even absent. Tell: what sleepiness changes is how long each episode lasts.

This reverses the pattern: rapid eye movement episodes lengthen as a person becomes more rested and shorten when the person is extremely sleepy. Tell: sleep debt shortens or removes the episodes, and rest lengthens them.
E.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 6

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
E.q: A 68-year-old man who has smoked for 50 years has 3 days of worsening dyspnea and wheezing. His chest film shows hyperinflation without vascular congestion, his arterial carbon dioxide is 61 mmHg (normal 35-45), and his B-type natriuretic peptide is 70 pg/mL (normal under 100). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema raises the natriuretic peptide sharply and shows congestion on the film. Tell: his natriuretic peptide is normal and his film shows hyperinflation without congestion.
ruled out by a stated finding

A heart failure exacerbation gives a highly elevated natriuretic peptide, echocardiographic abnormalities and Kerley B lines (fluid in the interlobular septa). Tell: his natriuretic peptide is under 100 pg/mL.
ruled out by a stated finding

Embolism shows clear lungs and a normal natriuretic peptide early on, often with right ventricular strain on the electrocardiogram. Tell: his wheezing, hyperinflation and high carbon dioxide point to his airways instead.

Correct. Wheezing, hyperinflation on the chest film and hypercapnia point to an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and the natriuretic peptide is usually normal in that setting, as his is. Dyspnea, hypoxemia and tachycardia are shared with heart failure and embolism, so these features decide.

E.topic: Aspiration, chest tube, pleurodesis and surgery
E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
E.q: A 30-year-old woman is scheduled for pleurodesis after her third spontaneous pneumothorax. She asks what the procedure will do inside her chest. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: A Heimlich valve is a one-way flutter valve that lets air escape through a chest tube. Tell: draining air empties the space for now, whereas pleurodesis obliterates the space so the lung cannot collapse away again.

Correct. Pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space by inducing inflammation there: an irritant causes adhesions of the two layers of pleura, which helps keep the lung inflated after pneumothorax and leaves no room for fluid in an effusion. It is used to prevent recurrent or treat resistant pneumothorax.

Stapling or resection of blebs is a separate step performed during video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery. Tell: pleurodesis bonds the parietal and visceral layers together; it does not close the blebs themselves.

Mechanical pleurodesis abrades the pleura and chemical pleurodesis instills a sclerosant such as talc; neither removes a layer. Tell: the goal is irritation that makes the two layers adhere, not taking either one away.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
E.q: A 47-year-old woman has months of episodes of skin flushing, watery diarrhea with cramps, and wheezing. Exam shows an enlarged liver and a heart murmur, and echocardiography shows thickening of the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. Computed tomography shows a mass in a bronchus. Which tumor is most likely?
opts: Small cell carcinoma has neuroendocrine paraneoplastic effects, but its classic syndrome is inappropriate antidiuretic hormone with low sodium and confusion. Tell: flushing, diarrhea and right-sided valve thickening are serotonin effects of carcinoid syndrome.

Squamous cell carcinoma is a central bronchial tumor whose particular paraneoplastic finding is hypercalcemia. Tell: flushing with diarrhea and tricuspid and pulmonic valve thickening is carcinoid syndrome from serotonin.

Adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral, with cough and shortness of breath early and bone pain and weight loss later. Tell: episodic flushing, diarrhea and right-sided valve disease are the serotonin picture of a bronchial carcinoid.

Correct. Carcinoid syndrome, which in the lung arises mainly from a bronchial carcinoid, comes from release of serotonin by the tumor cells. Its features include cutaneous flushes, diarrhea, cramps, nausea and vomiting, cough, wheezing and dyspnea, hepatomegaly, and pulmonic and tricuspid valve thickening and stenosis, matching her picture.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
E.q: A 58-year-old man who smokes 2 packs a day is worried after his brother was diagnosed with lung cancer. He asks which type of lung cancer is most strongly associated with smoking. Which response is accurate?
opts: Large cell carcinoma is a peripheral non-small cell cancer known for unusual metastases to the small intestine and bowel. Tell: it is not the type singled out for the strongest smoking association; squamous cell carcinoma is.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer, but it is not the type singled out for the strongest association with smoking. Tell: the strongest smoking link belongs to squamous cell carcinoma, the second most common type.

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma, the second most common lung cancer, has the strongest association with smoking. Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of all lung cancers and compounds with packs per day and years, but among the cell types it is squamous cell carcinoma that is singled out as most strongly tied to smoking.
A bronchial carcinoid is a rare type, known for carcinoid syndrome from serotonin release. Tell: the cancer singled out for the strongest association with smoking is squamous cell carcinoma.

E.topic: Pulmonary embolism: risk factors and presentation
E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary vascular diseases: 2. Cor pulmonale 3. Pulmonary embolism 4. Pulmonary hypertension 5. Pulmonary edema
E.q: What does the S1Q3T3 pattern on the electrocardiogram suggest?
opts: Correct. The S1Q3T3 pattern, a deep S wave in lead I with a Q wave and an inverted T wave in lead III, suggests severe right ventricular strain, not purely pulmonary embolism. It is highly specific but has low sensitivity, so its absence does not exclude embolism.

S1Q3T3 suggests severe right ventricular strain; it says nothing about a thickened left ventricle. Tell: a tall R wave in V1 marks right ventricular hypertrophy, and S1Q3T3 marks right ventricular strain.
Right atrial enlargement shows as peaked P waves, a separate electrocardiogram finding. Tell: S1Q3T3 is built from the S, Q and T waves, not the P wave, and it points to the right ventricle.

The pattern suggests severe right ventricular strain, not purely pulmonary embolism, so it does not name the diagnosis by itself. Tell: S1Q3T3 says the right ventricle is strained, whatever the cause.

E.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
E.q: A 20-year-old student plans to sleep 3 hours a night for the 4 nights before an exam, reasoning that nobody knows what sleep is for anyway. What should he be told?
opts: Sleep's role is unknown, so cutting it is safe

Researchers have limited understanding of why sleep is essential, but its importance is not in doubt: restriction over a few days already decreases performance. Tell: unknown mechanisms do not mean no effect.
Short nights can impair his thinking

Correct. Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease cognitive and physical performance, productivity and health, and the functions of sleep include cognition and the facilitation of learning or memory. Four nights of 3 hours is restriction over a few days, so his studying could backfire.
Short sleep mainly costs physical strength

Restriction lowers physical performance, but it lowers cognitive performance too, and sleep supports cognition and learning or memory. Tell: for exam preparation, the cognitive cost is the one that matters, and it is part of the expected effect.
Harm needs months of short sleep

Restriction over a few days is enough to decrease cognitive and physical performance, productivity and health. Tell: 4 short nights fall within that window, so harm is expected well before months have passed.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 52-year-old man is sedated on a mechanical ventilator after abdominal surgery. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.55 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 26 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 22 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which ventilator change is most appropriate?
opts: Lower the set rate or tidal volume

Correct. A pH of 7.55 with a carbon dioxide of 26 is a respiratory alkalosis, and on a ventilator the fix is to decrease minute volume by lowering the number of breaths per minute or the tidal volume, so less carbon dioxide is blown off.

Fluid and potassium replacement treat a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. His bicarbonate is 22 and the low carbon dioxide drives the pH. Tell: a respiratory alkalosis is fixed at the ventilator.
Leave the settings; mild alkalosis needs nothing
Treatment is usually not required only for a mild change, a pH below 7.50. His pH is 7.55. Tell: above 7.50 on a ventilator, decrease minute volume.
Raise the set rate or tidal volume

Raising rate or tidal volume increases minute volume and blows off more carbon dioxide, deepening the alkalosis. His carbon dioxide is already 26. Tell: too much ventilation is the problem, so turn it down.
E.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 38, 40

E.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
E.q: In the proposed theory, what ends a long period of wakefulness?
opts: Increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure and a slow heart rate, is a physiologic change during non-rapid eye movement sleep, a result of sleep rather than the trigger that ends wakefulness. Tell: the trigger is activating-neuron fatigue.

Correct. After the brain has remained active for many hours, neurons in the activating system become fatigued. The positive feedback cycle between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers take over.

Positive feedback between the reticular nuclei and the cortex is what sustains wakefulness; after many hours awake it fades rather than strengthens. Tell: sleep comes when the feedback weakens, so a stronger loop would prolong waking.

Release of the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition happens when the sleep centers are not activated, and it starts wakefulness rather than ending it. Tell: release from inhibition begins waking; fatigue of the activating neurons ends it.
E.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 14, 18, 19

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
E.q: A 25-year-old man presents with his second primary spontaneous pneumothorax on the right; the first was treated 18 months ago. He is stable. Which management best prevents further recurrence?
opts: Recurrent pneumothorax is on the list of contraindications to catheter aspiration. Tell: his is a second episode, and aspiration does nothing to prevent a third.
ruled out by a stated finding
Observation with oxygen fits a small first primary pneumothorax with minimal symptoms. Tell: a recurrence calls for definitive prevention, which observation does not provide.

Correct. A recurrent primary spontaneous pneumothorax calls for surgical therapy, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis, which is the best preventive procedure. Recurrence is common, approaching 50% within three years after a first episode, and his second episode proves the risk.
A chest tube evacuates the space in a large symptomatic episode but leaves the pleural space open to recur. Tell: for a recurrent primary pneumothorax the plan is surgery with pleurodesis.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
E.q: A 58-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has not been helped by continuous positive airway pressure or an oral appliance. He asks which operation would be a cure. Which procedure is described as a cure for obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Correct. Tracheostomy is a cure for obstructive sleep apnea because the site of upper airway obstruction is bypassed. Breathing no longer depends on the narrowed upper airway that collapses during sleep.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful in obstructive sleep apnea, a weaker claim than a cure. Tell: the procedure called a cure is the one that bypasses the site of obstruction, tracheostomy.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate disease when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: it is a treatment option; tracheostomy, which bypasses the obstruction, is the one called a cure.

Palatal implants are an option in mild obstructive sleep apnea for patients who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: they treat mild disease; the cure comes from bypassing the upper airway obstruction.
E.cite: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 13

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary neoplasms: 2. Pulmonary nodule 3. Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) a. Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) b. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) c. Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors 4. Paraneoplastic Neoplasm Associated Syndromes a. SIADH b. Hypercalcemia
E.q: A 63-year-old woman with a 35 pack-year history has a 9-mm solid nodule in the right upper lobe found on computed tomography for abdominal pain. Which additional feature of the nodule would most raise concern for malignancy?
opts: Central calcification is a benign pattern, typical of a healed granuloma. Tell: malignant calcification patterns are eccentric or stippled ground-glass, and a spiky border is the feature that raises concern most here.

Correct. Concerning nodules are greater than 6 mm, sit in the upper lobes or hilar structures, have a spiculated appearance (spikes, deviations or lobulations in the border), number more than 3, enlarge over time, enhance with contrast, appear cavitated or nonsolid, or occur in high-risk patients. A spiky border would add to her size, location and smoking.
Popcorn-looking calcification points to a hamartoma. Tell: it is a benign pattern, so it would lower concern; the concerning border is spiky or lobulated.
Fatty tissue inside a nodule points to a hamartoma and is a benign feature. Tell: fat reassures rather than alarms, while a spiculated border is a classic sign of a concerning nodule.

E.q: A 58-year-old man has 3 days of mild pleuritic chest pain. His Wells score is 1.5 (heart rate 104/min). His oxygen saturation is 97%, and he has no hemoptysis, no estrogen use, no prior clots, no recent surgery or trauma and no leg swelling. Because he fails the PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria), a D-dimer is sent, and it is 310 ng/mL (normal under 500 ng/mL). Which step fits?
opts: Computed tomographic angiography follows a positive D-dimer or a Wells score above 4. Tell: his D-dimer is below the cut-off and his Wells score is 1.5.
Repeating a negative D-dimer adds nothing: its high sensitivity is what makes a negative result safe to act on. Tell: the algorithm ends at a negative D-dimer.
A ventilation-perfusion scan is imaging for patients who need it but cannot have contrast. Tell: a negative D-dimer in a low-probability patient means he needs no imaging at all.

Correct. He fails two criteria (age 58 and heart rate 104/min), so a D-dimer was right with a Wells score of 4 or less. The D-dimer has high sensitivity, and a negative result safely excludes embolism in this low-probability outpatient, so no imaging is needed.
