E.q: A 41-year-old woman with sarcoidosis has a chest film showing diffuse reticular infiltrates throughout both lungs. Her previously enlarged hilar nodes are no longer seen, and there is no honeycombing or hilar retraction. Which radiographic stage is this?
opts: Stage I is bilateral hilar adenopathy alone with clear lungs. Tell: her hilar nodes are no longer enlarged and her lungs carry diffuse infiltrates, the opposite pattern to stage I in both features.
Stage II needs hilar adenopathy and parenchymal involvement together. Tell: her hilar nodes are no longer seen, leaving parenchymal disease alone, which is stage III rather than stage II.

Correct. Stage III is parenchymal involvement alone, seen as diffuse reticular infiltrates, with no hilar adenopathy. Her film has infiltrates without enlarged nodes and without the honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae or cysts that would mark stage IV.

Stage IV is advanced fibrosis with honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts or emphysema. Tell: her film has none of these, only diffuse reticular infiltrates, so she has not reached the fibrotic stage.

E.topic: Identifying the disorder step by step
E.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 58-year-old man is brought in confused with a low blood pressure, and the cause of his critical illness is not yet clear. Which initial testing best characterizes his acid-base status?
opts: Urine chloride before any blood testing
Urine chloride is used when a metabolic alkalosis has an unclear cause, after the blood gas has named the disorder. Tell: the blood gas and electrolytes come first.
Arterial gas and electrolytes drawn together

Correct. The first step is to obtain an arterial blood gas and electrolytes simultaneously, so the bicarbonate on each can be compared to verify accuracy and the anion gap can be calculated. In a critically ill patient the acid-base type can assist the diagnosis.
Electrolytes alone, adding a gas if abnormal
The anion gap can be abnormal even when sodium, chloride and bicarbonate are normal, and electrolytes alone give no pH or carbon dioxide. Tell: the disorder cannot be named without the gas.
Arterial gas now, electrolytes the next day
Drawing them a day apart loses the comparison of the two bicarbonate values and makes the anion gap unreliable. Tell: the gas and electrolytes are drawn at the same time.

E.q: A 71-year-old woman with cor pulmonale from interstitial lung disease has ankle edema and mild ascites. Her blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg and her potassium is 4.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5-5.0). A loop diuretic is started. Which approach to her diuresis should be avoided?
opts: Spironolactone is one of the diuretics used for the fluid retention of cor pulmonale, alongside loop diuretics. Tell: the danger is the pace of volume removal, not which diuretic is chosen.
Monitoring potassium is wise, because hypokalemia on loop diuretics can trigger lethal arrhythmias. Tell: checking potassium is a safety step to keep, not one to avoid.

Careful diuresis is the recommended approach: it treats the fluid retention of right ventricular failure while protecting preload. Tell: the error to avoid is the aggressive version, not diuresis itself.

Correct. The damaged right ventricle relies on elevated filling pressure (preload) to keep output up. Removing volume too aggressively drops that preload and starves the left ventricle, and output can fall catastrophically. Careful, monitored diuresis treats her edema without crashing her output.

E.topic: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and pulmonary fibrosis

E.q: A 72-year-old man with no occupational, drug or connective tissue disease history has 2 years of insidious dry cough and exertional dyspnea. He has bibasilar inspiratory crackles, pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern, chest films over several years show progressive fibrosis, and high-resolution computed tomography shows diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. How should the diagnosis be established?
opts: Correct. Over age 65, idiopathic disease with inspiratory crackles, restrictive physiology, radiographic progressive fibrosis over several years and diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography give idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with 90% confidence. Such patients do not need surgical lung biopsy.

Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy when the picture is incomplete. Tell: he is over 65 and meets all four criteria, which is the situation in which surgical lung biopsy is not needed for the diagnosis.

Transbronchial lung biopsy or fine-needle node biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas confirms sarcoidosis. Tell: he has no hilar adenopathy or multi-organ findings; his age and honeycombing fit idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which needs no biopsy here.

Antibodies to an inhaled agent in serum give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, after an organic dust exposure. Tell: he has no exposures, and his findings are the four criteria for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis instead.

E.q: A 19-year-old man is resuscitated after a near-drowning. Within 24 hours he has refractory hypoxemia and new bilateral opacities on chest film with a normal heart size, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. On the ventilator his arterial oxygen pressure is 54 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.60. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The criterion is met whenever the ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen is under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 54 / 0.60 = 90, far below 300, so he clearly meets the oxygenation criterion and sits in the worst class.

Mild is a ratio of 200-300 mm Hg, the least impaired class that still meets the criterion. Tell: his ratio of 54 / 0.60 = 90 is less than half the bottom of the mild range, two classes worse than mild.
Moderate covers 100-200 mm Hg. Tell: 54 / 0.60 = 90 falls just under 100, which crosses into the severe class; rounding up toward 100 is the mistake that makes moderate look right.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 54 / 0.60 = 90 mm Hg. A ratio under 100 is the severe class. Near-drowning is a direct pulmonary insult, and new bilateral opacities within a day with a normal heart complete the criteria.

E.q: A 57-year-old coal miner with complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis has progressive dyspnea. Which pulmonary function pattern, including the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide, is expected?
opts: Normal-looking results fit simple disease at most, where pulmonary function testing can be unimpressive. Tell: his complicated disease is restrictive, and the diffusing capacity falls rather than rises as scarring impairs gas transfer.

Correct. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis produces restrictive dysfunction with a reduced diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide. Simple disease can leave testing unimpressive, but his complicated, symptomatic disease brings the restrictive pattern and impaired gas transfer.

His dust-scarred lungs produce restrictive dysfunction, and the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide is reduced, not raised. Tell: both halves of this answer run opposite to the expected result in coal workers' pneumoconiosis.

Restriction is right, but scarring reduces the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide rather than raising it. Tell: the expected pairing in coal workers' pneumoconiosis is restriction with a low diffusing capacity.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 33-year-old woman with self-induced vomiting has a metabolic alkalosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.51 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her potassium is 2.9 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Her vomiting has stopped and saline has been started. Which approach to her potassium should be avoided?
opts: Rechecking potassium as the alkalosis corrects
Rechecking is how overcorrection is avoided, since potassium moves back out of cells as the pH falls. Tell: monitoring is the safe practice, not the one to avoid.
Treating the cause of her vomiting
Treating the underlying condition is the first step for metabolic alkalosis. Tell: the item to avoid is excess potassium, not care of the cause.
Replacing well beyond the measured deficit

Correct. Much of the low potassium in alkalosis is a shift into cells. Potassium deficits are treated if needed, but overcorrection is to be avoided, because as the alkalosis corrects potassium shifts back out of the cells.
Treating fluid and potassium deficits is part of treating saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and her potassium of 2.9 is low. Tell: replacement is right; overshooting is the danger.
